title: Fraser officially enters Carlton coaching race after mid-year turnaround
text:
Josh Fraser has presented to the Carlton hierarchy after officially entering the club's process to find its full-time coach.

After a stunning run of 10 wins from 12 matches since becoming interim coach when Michael Voss left the club in May, Fraser has Carlton on the cusp of the most unlikely finals appearance.

Although he has delivered a perfect on-the-job audition, Fraser was still required to pitch to the Blues' coaching panel on Wednesday.

Loading...

Untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) have been through the process, with Fraser only formally putting his hand up this week.

"A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process," Fraser said today.

"Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.

"I presented to the coaching panel this week."

At his first press conference when taking over from Voss, Fraser was adamant he was not interested in being Carlton's coach beyond this season.

But after a wildly successful 12 weeks in charge, buoyed by enthusiastic fans, Fraser could not turn down the opportunity.

"I have said, previously, that I've been ambitious to be a senior coach," Fraser said.

"I've been fortunate to be able to sit in the chair and consolidate some of my thinking; get some opportunity exposure to the role that otherwise you wouldn't normally get.

"It's been something that's been crystallising in my mind and my thoughts.

"Really confident that I'm ready to assume the responsibility of being a senior coach.

"There are 19 jobs to be a senior (AFL) coach.

"I'm as excited about this group as a lot of our Carlton supporters will be."

Joyous Blues fans were chanting "we want Fraser" as the Blues steamrolled St Kilda on Sunday night to put themselves in the box seat to earn a spot in the wildcard round.

If they defeat the Western Bulldogs, who will be without superstar captain Marcus Bontempelli on Sunday, the Blues will lock in their spot in the top 10.

It has been one of the more remarkable in-season turnarounds in AFL history, with Carlton 1-8 when Fraser took over.

"It can disrupt the club at times, when there's a significant change, like when you lose a coach, and you bring another coach in mid-season," Fraser said.

"That speaks to the culture that's been here, but I'm grateful for all the support I've had around me."

AAP

title: Breaking: Young Talent Time host Johnny Young dies
text:
Young Talent Time host Johnny Young has died aged 79 following a brief battle with pancreatic cancer.

"Johnny was the creator, host and producer of the much-loved television show Young Talent Time," his family said in a statement.

"He wrote and produced many iconic hit songs, including The Real Thing and Smiley."

Young Talent Time, a popular entertainment show, ran from 1971 until 1988 and nurtured a number of big Australian stars, including Dannii Minogue and Tina Arena.

Tina Arena was one of the young stars of Young Talent Time, hosted by Johnny Young. (Sergio Dionisio: AAP)

Each episode of Young Talent Time finished with a singalong of The Beatles' All My Loving.

Young was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2010, with Arena paying tribute to him at the ceremony by singing one of his tracks, Here Comes The Star, and describing him as "like a father" for the faith he showed when nurturing her skills on Young Talent Time.

"He's a dear man and I've never hidden the fact that he's the reason I'm still here 30 years later," she said at the time.

Before hosting Young Talent Time, Young was a singer in his own right, having an Australian number one hit with Step Back.

He was also the host of The Go!! Show in the 1960s, following the resignation of Ian Turpie.

Young won a Logie for Best Teenage Personality for his work on The Go!! Show in 1967.

Johnny Young won a Logie for his work hosting The Go!! Show. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

Young leaves behind his wife Marisha, sister Cornelia, daughters Anna and Fleur, seven grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren. He also had a son, Craig, who had died.

His family asked for privacy and said the details of a memorial service would be announced soon.

Johnny Young was born Johnny Benjamin De Jong.

title: Live: Are you priced out of a home? Australians share their stories
text:
Hearing the property market is in a downturn might make you ask: "Isn't that good for first home owners?"

But according to Cotality's Gerard Burg most of the properties getting cheaper aren't the ones first home buyers can afford.

"The initial declines across every city have been led by the highest value properties," he said.

Burg said the housing market is split into the top 25% of homes by value, the middle 50% and the lower 25%.

(ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

In markets like Brisbane and Adelaide, where the downturn has only just begun, only the top 25% of properties have begun to decrease in price.

"The lower quartile properties — the most likely to be purchased by first home buyers — are still increasing in value," he said.

In Sydney and Melbourne the cost of the lower quartile has only just begun to fall.

title: Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan quitting politics
text:
Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan has announced she's leaving politics, after stepping down from the Labor leadership just over a fortnight ago.

The member for Bendigo East called a press conference in her central Victorian seat on Friday morning to say she would not be contesting the November election.

Ms Allan has spent half her life in Victoria's parliament after first being elected in 1999, on the day before her 26th birthday.

Jacinta Allan's parents celebrate with her on the night she was elected to parliament. (X: Jacinta Allan)

She was Victoria's youngest-ever woman MP and ascended to the ministry when she was just 29.

"I am proud to say I didn't waste a day," Ms Allan said.

"With each day, I lived the values outlined in my first speech to parliament — quality investments in public health and education, a strong union movement, respect for other people and the role of the community in decision making.

"Fighting for decent jobs with decent wages is what must sit at the centre of what Labor governments deliver."

She said she had reflected on the current state of democracy as a former premier of Victoria and the state's longest serving female minister in any government in Australia.

"I do not remember a time when our foundations have felt so unsteady," she said.

"Social cohesion is under pressure, social debate is deteriorating.

"The line between truth and lie is becoming increasingly blurred and it's not just about politics, it's about how we live together, how we disagree, how we listen, how we turn pride in this country without turning that pride against each other."

Ms Allan said First Nations people were being denigrated and migrants demanded to fit in, women were held to standards that were not being applied equally.

She urged the community not to let fear and division be rewarded, fall for fake AI images and vision, and not to let the erosion of trust weaken democracy.

Ben Carroll was deputy premier to Jacinta Allan before taking the state's top job. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

She became premier in September 2023, when her predecessor Daniel Andrews quit politics.

On July 27, she stood down as Labor leader after losing the confidence of the majority of her party.

Her deputy, Ben Carroll, became the premier.

Jacinta Allan becomes emotional as she thanks supporters

Ms Allan singled out a number of community groups to thank.

They included Eaglehawk Community House who provided meals and support to vulnerable members of the Bendigo community, the CFA firefighters and volunteers who risked their lives to protect others and property.

"The kindness of strangers who stopped and thanked me for being their MP and encouraged me to keep going despite the hate," she said with her voice breaking.

Jacinta Allan used her press conference to thank her supporters and list her achievements for her hometown. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Ms Allan spoke proudly about being approached by a Bendigo high school student not long after being first elected who asked for her business card.

"[She] looked at it, looked at me and declared, 'Well if you can do it, so can I'."

"I've shown young boys and girls that you can live in Bendigo and run the state; that their premier is a person just like them or their mum, and that being a member of parliament or premier is not out of reach because you don't live in Melbourne or you don't go to a particular school."

She thanked her family, saying there were not enough words to express how much she loved them.

She said she looked forward to taking everything she had learnt and loved from politics into her next chapter.

Ms Allan did not take questions after her announcement.

Premier Ben Carroll paid tribute to his predecessor on ABC radio this morning, saying Jacinta Allan had transformed Bendigo. (ABC News: Laura Mayers)

Mr Carroll this morning paid tribute to Ms Allan during an interview with ABC regional radio.

"She has served the Bendigo and Victorian community for 27 years," he told Statewide Mornings.

"She's transformed Bendigo for the better … I wish her every success in the future."

Ms Allan also announced her retirement from politics on social media.

"I was young. I was nervous. But I knew exactly why I was there," she wrote about winning her first election.

"In my first speech to Parliament, I said I wanted to be a representative who cared about people and listened to them."

Amongst the achievements she listed from her three decades as Bendigo's representative were the redevelopment of the Bendigo Hospital, upgrades to state schools in the district, new local train stations and the establishment of government services hub in the regional city.

"There are no words big enough to describe what this community means to me," she wrote.

"It's where I learnt who I was fighting for."

She said that politics had not only changed since she was elected, but that she also had.

"I became a wife. A mum. A minister. A deputy premier. And premier of the greatest state in the country."

She described her husband and two children as her greatest supporters and her greatest joy.

"There were extraordinary days. There were bloody hard ones too," she said.

"But through all of it, I never forgot who sent me there — or why. And when I leave Parliament, I'll leave the same way I arrived. A daughter of Bendigo. A daughter of workers. A proud Labor woman."

title: Research uncovers what determines flavour of Australian chocolate
text:
As the Australian cocoa industry continues to gain momentum, new research has emerged to help identify and market regional flavour profiles.

Researchers have found where beans are fermented can have an even greater influence on the flavour of a finished chocolate bar than the cocoa trees themselves.

In a project conducted by the University of Queensland in collaboration with local growers, researchers found clear differences in the flavour of cocoa fermented at three Far North Queensland locations: Mossman, Fishery Falls and Mission Beach.

Mission Beach cocoa farmer and chocolate maker Chris Jahnke supplied the crop used in the trials.

He said the results scientifically backed some of what he had already suspected and found fermentation could account for almost half of the flavour produced in a chocolate bar.

Chris Jahnke is an Australian cocoa farmer and chocolate maker. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

The trials notably produced different flavour profiles in the cocoa from each fermentation site.

"The Mossman [cocoa] had a more fruity profile, the Mission Beach one had a more chocolatey profile, and the Fishery Falls one was kind of in between those," Mr Jahnke said.

He said this could provide Australian cocoa producers with a point of difference.

"Predominantly, it's a kind of a marketing approach because in Australia … we concentrate on producing a premium chocolate product," Mr Jahnke said.

Fermentation detemines about half of the flavour in chocolate. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Fermenting cocoa

UQ food chemist Marlize Bekker said fermentation affected flavour through the activity of microorganisms naturally present in the environment.

"You have all these small microorganisms and, during fermentation, they produce a lot of metabolites," Dr Bekker said.

"It's their metabolites that produce all those precursor compounds that can later be transformed into cocoa flavour and more roasted flavour, sometimes a buttery flavour and even a tropical fruit flavour."

Cocoa is fermented out in the open using wild yeasts. (Supplied: Chris Jahnke)

A metabolite is a substance produced when microorganisms break down nutrients during fermentation.

Unlike some other fermenting processes, cocoa is generally fermented using naturally occurring microorganisms rather than a specific yeast strain.

That means the environment where cocoa is fermented can influence which microorganisms are active and, ultimately, how the chocolate tastes.

Mr Jahnke is keen to explore further research into how fermentation changes between seasons and which yeasts are active at different stages of the process.

Cocoa beans are surrounded by a sweet, sticky substance when removed from the pod, which contributes to the fermentation process. (Supplied: Chris Jahnke)

Regional flavour

Jim McKerlie is executive chair of the Australian Cocoa Group, which is working to expand Australia's cocoa industry.

He said the research could eventually help consumers choose chocolate based on its regional flavour profile, much like they might choose a wine based on where it was produced.

"People in the future would be able to say, 'Well I've got this cocoa, this is from Tully and we know that from Tully it's got these particular flavour profiles,'" Mr McKerlie said.

" You can go up and down that cocoa belt … and find different flavour profiles. "

Mr McKerlie said understanding the link between location and flavour could also influence how growers approached production.

Fermentation location contributes more to chocolate flavour than the cocoa plant itself, research has found. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

"As the cocoa industry expands … [growers] are going to be much more cognisant of the potential flavour profile they can produce."

He added that Australian cocoa was marketed at a premium price compared to international bulk cocoa, and this research could help explain why.

"One of the factors that will justify that differentiation or that premium is the fact that you can say this is where it's come from, this is the flavour profile that you get, and consumers love that."

title: Farmers rejoice as 'once-in-a-lifetime' wet season follows drought
text:
After successive years of devastating drought, South Australia's grain farmers say they are now experiencing some of the best conditions for growing crops in their lifetime.

Some farms have already received more than double their total rainfall for 2024 and 2025, while further rain at the start of August has pushed optimism for a bumper harvest to new heights.

While there are still several weeks left of the growing season and frost remains a risk, farmers say the potential for a big SA grain crop is "massive" after the past two dry years pushed many growers to the wall.

On parts of the state's Eyre Peninsula, some farmers have almost tripled last year's rainfall.

Mr Williams says recent rain has "set us up for spring" – a most crucial time for crops. (ABC Rural: Brooke Neindorf)

Streaky Bay farmer Dion Williams said the more than 400mm of rain he has received so far this year was a "staggering" amount for the district.

"I've been doing this for 28 years and I honestly feel like this could be a once-in-a-lifetime year … personally, as a family farm," Mr Williams said.

"Everyone's taking photos of their crops and sharing them, and I'm all for it, it's great. You've got to celebrate the good times."

Massive turnaround

He said 2026 was "chalk and cheese" compared to last year.

"When you get 120mm on the end of February, and everything starts to grow, your optimism starts to grow, especially after the last two years," Mr Williams said.

"We did get a get out of jail free card last year with some reasonable crops on the rainfall we had, but the year before was an absolute disaster."

Wheat crops are looking fantastic on SA's Eyre Peninsula after some very welcome rain. (Supplied: Dion Williams)

More than 400mm of rain has fallen in 2026 on Chris Lymn's farm at Wudinna, where he grows lentils and barley.

"Never before — haven't seen before in my time, so it's a fantastic year," Mr Lymn said.

"Early break, perfect conditions, crops in and up as early as you'd like to go — couldn't have asked for any better, really.

"We're all ready to make hay while the sun shines.

"We're a bit dubious as farmers to say we don't want more rain, but certainly we're a long way towards it. Normally we'd be looking for a September rain to finish; this rain this weekend means that we can probably just make do with a cool finish and we'll be pretty happy.

"We'd never say no, but I'd say we're pretty well home and hosed."

Confidence booming

Cungena farmer Miles Tomney received an early break of 138mm in late February — almost his total rainfall for 2024 in one event — and has since ticked over 450mm to date.

"It might be one out of the box we might not ever see again," Mr Tomney said.

"Confidence is up. Everyone's got a positive outlook at the moment, hopefully for everything the frosts stay away and everyone gets a piece of it [the rain].

"Everywhere I've driven across the state, no-one's missing out, so it's South Australia's turn by the looks."

Tim Paschke's paddocks were bare dirt and sand this time last year. (Supplied: Tim Paschke)

One district that has experienced a remarkable turnaround is SA's Riverland, where farmers this time last year were staring at bare, dusty paddocks.

Waikerie grower Tim Paschke is this year relieved to see healthy canola and lentil crops swaying in the breeze.

He described the more than 30mm of rain that fell on his farm in the past week as "a real blessing" at a critical time.

"[It's] one of the best August rains we can remember for such a long time, compared to last year when we didn't even have our paddocks covered," Mr Pashke said.

Mr Pashke grows canola, lentils, barley and wheat in the SA's Riverland. (Supplied: Tim Paschke)

"It's been an absolute game changer. When you get such a soaking rain, it does so much for the soil, and it's just such a load off our minds; we're very happy.

" There's some real positives for us, and obviously my bank balance really needs a bit of a kick because it's been three pretty tough years up here. "

The exact same paddocks that were bare in August 2025 are now lush, exactly a year later. (Supplied: Tim Paschke)

Agronomist Jake Hull believed some wheat crops could more than double the average yield this year — but cautioned that the season wasn't over yet.

"It is a sight to behold. The potential is massive," Mr Hull said.

"I like to keep reality in check, and we've still got a little way to go … but this last lot of rain has definitely raised that level of optimism to another level."

title: Albanese says Trump considering tariff exemption after phone call
text:
The prime minister has used a rare phone call with Donald Trump to press for an exemption from the administration's latest round of sweeping tariffs, saying the US president has agreed to give "consideration" to his request.

Anthony Albanese called a snap press conference this morning after an overnight phone call with Mr Trump, the first since their extraordinary late-night exchange in March over the fate of Iranian female footballers in Australia.

The ABC was told the call went for about 40 minutes, and Mr Albanese described the conversation as "productive, constructive … and substantial".

The federal government complained loudly in July when the Trump administration announced a 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from Australia as part of a global regime of import taxes on countries the US claims have failed to remove forced labour from supply chains.

New 12.5pc US tariff for Australia A new levy on exports from Australia into the US has taken effect, superseding the 10 per cent tariff that was expiring. Dozens of other countries have also been hit, but Australia's tariff is among the highest.

Australia maintains there is "no credible evidentiary basis" for the move, and senior government ministers believe the administration is simply trying to find a workaround after the Supreme Court struck down its 10 per cent tariffs in February.

Mr Albanese said he urged Mr Trump to "consider a full exemption" for Australia, or "at the very least no increase" from the old 10 per cent tariff rate.

"I informed him about our record when it comes to dealing with issues such as modern slavery, the strengthening that we have put forward as well, to look and hold companies accountable for the supply chain process as well," Mr Albanese said.

He said he did not put his request in "ideological" terms, but stressed the scale of Australian investment in the United States and that "over 20 years the US has had a trade surplus with Australia of US$442 billion".

"I put the argument very much to the president, as a friend of the United States, we would request that to be considered," he said.

" We have a different position when it comes to tariffs and, of course, our position as a government is that tariffs are an economic imposition and a cost on the countries that are imposing them. "

He did not sound optimistic about Mr Trump budging, saying the two sides have "a different view" on tariffs, but said the US president promised to give "consideration" to his request.

Leaders discuss Iran war and AUKUS

Anthony Albanese speaks to the media about his phone call with Donald Trump. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The two men also discussed the war in Iran, with Mr Albanese telling journalists that he reiterated Australia's call for the conflict to be brought to an end.

Analysts say the US is now stuck in a quagmire in Iran with no clear exit strategy, while talks over Tehran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz remain bogged down.

Mr Albanese said Mr Trump gave him an "extensive update" on the progress of the war, and "expressed his confidence going forward".

The two men also discussed AUKUS, with Mr Albanese saying they agreed the nuclear submarine program remained "full steam ahead".

And Mr Albanese told journalists that he raised China's recent ballistic missile test in the Pacific, which has stirred unease among several nations across the Pacific and has been sharply criticised by several Western nations and US allies.

He said Mr Trump responded by observing that the missile test "caused a great deal of concern right across the Pacific, which is true".

The prime minister said he also briefed the US president about the host of new treaties which Australia had struck across the Pacific recently.

title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
text:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly after the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was shown a red card for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after the La Liga side Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, the Premier League outfit walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on, believing a penalty shootout should decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

title: Payne's fame began as a joke. Now his shirt has sparked a bidding war
text:
Just a few months ago, few soccer fans outside New Zealand and Australia knew Tim Payne's name. Now they are bidding thousands of dollars for the jersey off his back.

The shirt Payne wore in his debut for Club Olimpia, a Paraguayan soccer powerhouse, has become a coveted piece of match-worn memorabilia since the club put it up for auction online five days ago.

With bidding set to close, the leading offer has climbed above 21 million in Paraguay's currency, the guarani, equivalent to around $5,000.

Viral Kiwi star meets Argentine influencer who boosted following to 5M New Zealand soccer player Tim Payne has met social media influencer Valen Scarsini after the Argentine encouraged his fans to follow the unheralded All Whites player.

It is the latest development in the unlikely rise of the 32-year-old defender, who entered the World Cup with just over 4,000 followers on Instagram and emerged as one of the tournament's biggest social media sensations.

Before representing New Zealand at the World Cup, Payne spent most of his career out of the limelight, playing for low-profile clubs in New Zealand before playing 143 A-League matches for Wellington. He also spent two years with England's Blackburn Rovers but never made a major appearance because of work-permit problems.

Then Argentine soccer influencer Valen Scarsini, known online as El Scarso, went searching for what he called the World Cup's "least-known soccer player".

Scarsini settled on Payne, whose Instagram account had 4,715 followers at the time, and encouraged his more than 2 million followers across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube to follow Payne, flood his posts with supportive comments and mention his name everywhere.

Loading Instagram content

Within days, Payne's following skyrocketed, eventually topping 5.4 million — more than the entire population of his native New Zealand. The surge in online fame helped carry Payne to Paraguay, where he signed with national club champion Olimpia on a one-year deal in June, ending a seven-year stint with Wellington Phoenix.

Payne gave legions of new fans another reason to cheer him during his August 2 debut against Asunción club Rubio Ñu, scoring minutes after coming off the bench to help Olimpia win 5-0.

Now the signed jersey from that match is drawing the sort of interest usually reserved for far more established names — though the leading offer remains a far cry from the millions of dollars paid for jerseys worn by Argentine superstar Lionel Messi and other soccer greats.

"I know exactly what it means to wear these stripes and play in this shirt, and that's why I want to give it to a true Olimpista (Olimpia fan)," Payne said in a video launching the auction.

AP

title: Kangaroo drownings in canal spark community concern
text:
Driving down a country road near the Riverina town of Nericon, the first thing that hits is the putrid smell.

WARNING: This story contains images of dead animals that may be distressing for readers.

Eight kangaroo carcasses are visible, five in the water and three on the bank side of the canal where they have all drowned.

"In winter it's actually gotten worse, I'm seeing more and more carcasses," said resident and bus driver Anita Tovo.

Anita Tovo says it is upsetting to see so many kangaroos dying when solutions exist. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

The high-density polyethylene (HDPE) sheets that line the banks of the Murrumbidgee Irrigation-owned canal were first installed in 2019 to prevent water loss.

Fencing was installed at the same time.

The plastic-lined canal and fencing trap the kangaroos, leaving them little opportunity to escape. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

"I never saw kangaroos in here … before the plastic lining and fencing [was installed]. I think it's about five years now that I've really taken notice," Ms Tovo said.

The only open area for kangaroos to exit the canal is a few kilometres further on where the fencing stops and rocks line the bank.

In a statement, Murrumbidgee Irrigation (MI) said fencing, cameras and escape structures known as egress points were in place at regular intervals along the canal and were being monitored.

"While these channels are essential for ensuring efficient and sustainable water use, we do acknowledge that they can unintentionally impact local wildlife," it said.

The only open area where kangaroos can escape is kilometres downstream, but many do not make it that far. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

While some cameras are visible at the canal, Ms Tovo said she was still finding dead kangaroos regularly.

"How many are dying, how many are being saved, how many are noticed going in and how quick are you [Murrumbidgee Irrigation] to come out to save them?" she said.

Ms Tovo said she had seen the occasional loosely placed rubber mat or rope ladder, but she said neither provided adequate assistance to the kangaroos.

The kangaroos that drown upstream end up floating down to the regulator. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

'Near impossible' for wildlife rescuers

WIRES spokesperson John Grant said when they started getting repeat reports about kangaroos in this canal, they knew something was not right.

"We don't tend to get a lot of calls about kangaroos in canals, certainly not like the amount that we've had with this," he said.

Mr Grant said resources are stretched in rural NSW and saving a drowning kangaroo was near impossible.

"Because our closest volunteer is at least an hour away from Nericon, when she arrived, twice I think it was that she went there, they had already drowned," he said.

Three kangaroos were pulled from the canal on New Farms Road after drowning. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Kangaroos are a protected species in every Australian state, and while it is not uncommon to see them on the roadside after being hit by a car, Mr Grant said this was different.

"This isn't a random accident," he said.

"This is an ongoing issue where these kangaroos continue to drown presumably because there isn't enough infrastructure for them to be able to get out of a canal that's been lined with black plastic."

There are currently no state regulations relating to egress points and animal welfare in canals.

Solutions available

Kylie Soanes says animal drownings in canals are a nationwide problem, with plastic lining exacerbating the issue. (ABC News: Rhiannon Stevens)

A research fellow in urban biodiversity at the University of Melbourne, Kylie Soanes, said waterway designs should keep native wildlife in mind.

"The ground is flat and then all of a sudden there's just a steep drop into this irrigation canal, and there's none of that sloping edge that would allow animals to escape that we might see in any kind of natural waterway," she said.

" It's very fair to say that the plastic exacerbates the danger of these canals. "

Dr Soanes said countries like the Netherlands, which is famous for its canals, were an example of what can be done to prevent these types of animal deaths.

"They [the Netherlands] cut escape ramps into the edge of the canal and line them with rocks and create a bit more of a slope," she said.

"So if an animal is drifting along a deep section of canal, they'll be able to find their feet and get out."

Dr Soanes said fencing was also an important solution to the problem, and while there was no one-size-fits-all fence for every animal, they should cater to the local wildlife.

"Because there's so much land on one side of the fence, they can get a good run up, which allows them to propel themselves over the fence and into the canal area. But once they're in, there's not a lot of wiggle room," she said.

"So it either needs to be high enough to completely exclude kangaroos … or there need to be escape ramps that allow any animals that have accidentally found themselves in the channel corridor to get themselves out."

Drowned kangaroos are a too-common sight in the Nericon canal. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Ms Tovo said something needed to change.

She said she and members of WIRES had met with Murray Irrigation to discuss the issues, but nothing further had come from the meeting.

"There's got to be consultation with [animal] welfare organisations because I'm sitting here and I can smell those carcasses and we can see what's happening because people don't care."

MI said it was committed to ongoing improvement and was continuing to assess infrastructure to identify further ways to enhance animal safety.

title: Qantas passengers stranded in Johannesburg for days demand compensation
text:
Exhausted Qantas passengers are demanding answers and compensation after a mechanical problem with their plane left them stranded in South Africa for days.

QF64 from Johannesburg to Sydney was due to depart OR Tambo International Airport on Monday night, local time, for the 12-hour journey back to Australia.

Instead, passengers say they were left in limbo and forced to scramble for their own accommodation after multiple attempts to depart were abandoned.

The super jumbo remains on the tarmac in the South African city undergoing repairs.

Qantas eventually sent another plane to bring them home, with hundreds arriving in Sydney last night.

Passenger Harriett Moore said the experience was "distressing".

Harriett Moore finally arrived home in Sydney last night. (Supplied)

"We had fellow passengers with children that ran out of nappies and formula, other passengers missed events like parties," Ms Moore said.

"We accept that safety must come first; however, why a near 50-hour delay has been met with limited explanation and an offer … that does not reflect the disruption, cost and distress involved."

A message from Qantas saying the flight has been cancelled. (Supplied)

In an email to passengers, Qantas said it had identified a problem with the aircraft's nose wheel.

It said the plane returned to the gate on August 10 for "engineering support" and on August 11 engineers "sourced and installed replacement parts from overseas" but "further work was needed to fully resolve the issue".

"On August 12, we secured a new aircraft to avoid any further delay. Safety will always be our highest priority," the email to passengers said.

Qantas initially offered Qantas Frequent Flyers 20,000 points, or a $200 "Customer Care Travel Voucher" for non-members on August 10, the day of the scheduled departure.

But after questions from the ABC, Qantas sent another email to customers as they landed back in Sydney yesterday, instead offering to refund the Johannesburg to Sydney leg as well as an Uber voucher home.

"On behalf of everyone at Qantas, we sincerely apologise for the significant disruption to your travel plans this week from Johannesburg," the email to passengers said.

"Thank you for your patience and understanding throughout what we know was an exceptionally difficult experience."

Passengers left in limbo

Ms Moore, who had been visiting family in South Africa, said the drama unfolded on Monday night.

"The captain told us there was something wrong with the nose gear, so we waited and waited, the plane pushed back, and then the captain came on again and said there was still an issue and we would have to disembark," Ms Moore said.

She said passengers scrambled for hotel rooms and were not assisted by the airline.

"The next morning we got a message saying our flight was leaving that afternoon, so we got back on board. We were then again told there were issues, and they were cancelling our flight, so we had to get off and go and find another hotel."

Ms Moore said Qantas' revised offer to refund one leg of the flight did not go far enough.

"There needs to be a change in regulations to compensate customers who are stranded like the EU does," she said.

" The cost of us now needing to take unpaid leave from work and missing critical meetings will not be compensated for a flight refund. "

The European Union requires airlines to pay passengers delayed by mechanical faults up to 600 euros ($980) in compensation.

Earlier this year, the federal government allocated $40 million to overhaul airline passenger rights.

Currently, Australia has no guaranteed compensation scheme for disrupted flights.

Questions over A380 safety

The disruption comes after Airbus was ordered in June to inspect 16 A380 aircraft, including one operated by Qantas, after cracks were found in a key structural component of the plane's wing.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency ordered the inspections after the cracks were discovered in a structural beam that carries significant aerodynamic loads.

There is no indication the Johannesburg aircraft's steering problem is related to those inspections.

Urgent inspections for cracks in A380s Airbus says it will inspect 16 A380 planes, including one Qantas plane, after cracks were found in a key wing component.

Qantas has also previously faced scrutiny over A380 maintenance, after a 1.25-metre tool was found inside one of its A380 engines following about 300 hours of flying.

Aviation expert Justin Wastnage said passengers should not be concerned about the safety of the A380.

"All aircraft are certified by the European safety agency, the Federal Aviation Administration, the US, our own CASA, and they all go through rigorous tests," he said.

"Flying is statistically still the safest form of travel, and the A380 is no different."

title: Brian To'o is still just the beginning for the PNG Chiefs
text:
After a week in the spotlight following the biggest decision of his career, Brian To'o went back to work.

His showing in the Panthers' 12-6 loss to the Roosters was typical of the To'o we've come to know.

The future Papua New Guinea Chief did not bring up his 100th try for the Panthers but did churn through 17 runs for 162 metres to go with five tackle busts and two line breaks. For some wingers that's a big night but for To'o it's the standard.

'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate Two of the NRL's most successful modern coaches weigh into the debate about the concessions afforded to the league's forthcoming PNG franchise.

The performance came in the days following confirmation of To'o's move to the Papua New Guinea Chiefs and it shouldn't have been a surprise.

There are good reasons To'o has become the premier winger of his time, and having such a high baseline is one of them.

Continued excellence on his part, for both the rest of this season and his final year with Penrith in 2027, is as close to a given as you'll find anywhere in rugby league.

He is the best player the Chiefs have signed but that may not remain so. Not since the Broncos filled their boots with Queensland-based stars for their inaugural season in 1988 has an expansion team signed so much established talent.

Zac Lomax will return to rugby league with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Brendon THorne)

Of the six players to commit to the Chiefs, four have played State of Origin in the past two years. Some clubs go decades without signing one or two players who fit such a criteria.

The other two are the greatest try-scorer the Australian game has ever known and one of England's top front-rowers.

Unless Joseph Manu was just in Port Moresby on holiday, it seems likely they'll add the Golden Boot winner from the most recent World Cup to the list before long.

They have achieved all this without really entering the cut and thrust of the transfer market in earnest. Officially, the Chiefs cannot talk to any NRL free agents for the 2028 season until November 1 this year.

Manu has been linked with an NRL return with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Each of the signings they've made within the NRL have come because a club granted permission for the player in question to negotiate early or because the player activated something in their contract that allowed them to do so.

They've done all this while the luxury compound they're building is still a hole in the ground and before they have a logo or a jersey. To'o himself hasn't even been to Papua New Guinea before.

They're yet to land any young legs but if these are the players they can sign through the activation of obscure clauses and arcane options and the like, imagine what they can do in the jungle of true free agency when they have the biggest and sharpest teeth via their mountain of government funding?

With local products like Gairo Voro, Morea Morea and Finlay Glare, all of whom are enjoying standout seasons with London Broncos and will eventually take up development contracts with the club, to fill out the other end of the roster, the Cheifs can keep aiming high.

The floodgates have yet to truly open but already the ripples of the league's new money-monster are clear to see.

Hudson Young, fresh off a career-changing State of Origin series, is in the Chiefs' sights and despite the Raiders offering just about everything they've got to a player who has found a home in Canberra, fans there are turning as green as their jerseys because they know there's a chance they'll be money-whipped.

Young is the latest player to come into PNG's sights. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The spectre of similar moves loom over a sport addicted to transfer gossip and sank into Thursday's top-of-the-table clash because after the start they've made, no player seems out of reach for the Chiefs.

Not Sam Walker, who turned down the Roosters first contract offer midweek and has the chance to secure untold riches over the final stages of this season, a chance he has surely enhanced after a mature performance that helped put the Tricolours on top of the ladder.

Not Liam Martin, who rattled Cody Ramsey with the best shot of the night or Spencer Leniu, who struggled to find the fire against his former club and looks like he'd benefit from a change of scenery.

Not even Nathan Cleary, who tried every trick he knew but could not break down a resolute Roosters defensive line.

As impossible as it seems to picture him playing rugby league in anything but a Penrith jersey, even he is in play.

Through their tax-free contracts and the legitimacy that comes with signing established stars, the Chiefs have the capability to tip the entire league on its head.

They can pay a battler like a prince, a prince like a king and a king like a god and given they've already shown a taste for the finer things in assembling their roster, there's little reason to expect it won't continue.

Their advantages warp the salary cap beyond recognition and each signing they make is further proof of concept that the gold rush is real.

General manager of football Michael Chammas says he wears it as a badge of honour that clubs are beginning to gripe at the advantages PNG have been given and well may he, given how those clubs, blinded by the glittering of gold, let a Chief into the henhouse.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

It is hard to begrudge any player for taking what's on offer, like it's hard to begrudge the way Chammas and the Chiefs are going about it. They're playing by the rules they've been given and they're playing by them well.

Ever since Jarome Luai was announced as their first signing, their power has become more and more real and it continues to solidify with every signing they make. Now, they are securing a firm foothold on the high side of an uneven surface.

To'o is the latest, but not the last and rugby league is only just beginning to reckon with the power of what the NRL has created with its concessions to the Chiefs and how it alters the competitive balance of the league.

They have turned the dial as far as it will go and are now waiting to see what happens next, as is their way, and it is happening hard and fast all around us.

The downpour of money is a monsoon that shows no sign of breaking, even as rival clubs get swamped.

And stars like To'o who have been swept along are still just the start. Expect plenty more to dive in.

title: Teen Italian star breaks world record for second time this week
text:
Italian teenage swimming sensation Sara Curtis has broken the world 50m backstroke world record again, just a day after eclipsing the global mark of Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

The 19-year-old Curtis ‌won gold in 26.56 seconds in the final of the European Championships in Paris on Thursday, local time, clipping another 0.07 seconds off the time of 26.63 she had set in Wednesday's semifinals.

That time had obliterated the three-year-old mark of five-time Olympic champion McKeown, who had clocked 26.86 when winning a World Cup race in Budapest in 2023.

Teenager breaks Kaylee McKeown backstroke world record Italian teenager Sara Curtis has set a new world record in the women's 50m backstroke, beating the mark previously held by Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

It continued the historic week for the Savigliano-born Curtis, who has a Nigerian mother and Italian father, as she becomes the first Black swimmer to hold an individual long-course world record.

Mary-Ambre Moluh, from ​France, finished ‌half a second behind Curtis ​to take the silver, while Britain's Lauren Cox took ​bronze.

"I'm happy I managed it again. It's absurd, another crazy feat," Curtis told Italian TV station Rai 2.

It ​was the ​third medal in Paris for ‌the University of Virginia star, who also took bronze in 100m freestyle and silver in ​the 4x100m freestyle relay.

The teenager had been inching towards the ​world ​record all year, having ​broken the Italian and ‌European records earlier in the season.

"From the moment I set off for Virginia, that's all I thought about, the record. A dream and ​an immense goal," she admitted.

But it has been a tough spell for McKeown, who had to pull out of both the recent Commonwealth Games and the current Pan Pacific Championships because of glandular fever.

The 25-year-old is determined to get back into top shape for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, where Curtis shapes to be one of the pool stars.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki claimed the European 200m breaststroke gold, continuing his terrific rise.

The 18-year-old was fresh from winning gold for Jersey at the Commonwealth Games, only the second ever for his little Channel Island home.

title: ‘Has my team’s shooting improved?’ How AI is professionalising junior sport
text:
Advertisement

SportAI ‘Has my team’s shooting improved?’ How AI is professionalising junior sport Marc McGowan Updated August 14, 2026 — 12:26pm ,first published 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

During the dog days of Melbourne’s COVID-19 lockdowns, Sam Hung and his teenage friends would head to a local basketball court and shoot hoops to pass the time. Hung was a high school student back then, but already a budding technological guru. Collingwood junior basketballers are using stat-tracking app Superstat to get better. Jason South With so much time on his hands, he decided to build a basic app that produced shot charts from those street-ball games. Little did he know that experience would be helpful several years later, when he joined forces with Kai Bloomfield and Cordelia King to co-found Superstat. They created a stat-tracking app that uses artificial intelligence computer vision to deliver amateur sports teams – starting with basketball – the kind of performance data previously available only to elite athletes.

Advertisement

Related Article AI Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs Computer vision is an AI subfield that equips machines with the ability to process, analyse and interpret visual inputs such as images and videos, then extract meaningful information. Superstat just scored $3.5 million in seed funding from venture capital firm Blackbird and some private investors, and the team is relocating to Austin, Texas, in September to dive deeper into the United States market – a sports mecca that already is strongly featured among their membership – where they plan to expand to American football, baseball, soccer and volleyball. Closer to home, Australian football and netball are on the company’s hit list, too. “Our mission is to provide pro-level stats for everyone,” Bloomfield told this masthead.

Advertisement

NBA-level stats for amateurs The Melbourne entrepreneurs first worked together on a different app, TrainStop, a sports recruiting matchmaker that was once described as football’s answer to Tinder. The app proved popular with grassroots clubs, but a problem soon surfaced: would-be recruits were “catfishing” them, embellishing their output to try to earn a quick buck. Superstat co-founders Sam Hung, Cordelia King and Kai Bloomfield use AI technology to deliver professional-level statistics for amateur athletes. Eddie Jim Bloomfield, an ex-Oakleigh Chargers development coach in the under-18 Talent League who was working at St Kilda as a football analyst at the time, realised there was a missing link – and it owed to a lack of data.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Australian Open AI analysed Jannik Sinner’s skeleton. This is what it found He was manually “cutting” footage for the Saints, an onerous task mirrored at amateur level, where coaches and fellow volunteers were more time poor and unable to gather the same level of information. Hence, some mischievous TrainStop members saw an opportunity to use that data deficit to their advantage. That was when Bloomfield and co. started wondering about the possibility of using AI to track statistics and plug that gap in grassroots sport. Superstat effectively became the app designed to solve that problem. The company’s early days last year were devoted to football before they found out about Hung’s basketball app from the pandemic.

Advertisement

That was enough for them to pivot to basketball – but it wasn’t until they started attending tournaments and speaking to people involved that they realised the opportunity at hand. The trio recalled a photo they took from the annual Adelaide Easter Classic, where there were four mobile phones positioned on tripods around a court recording a single junior basketball match. Bloomfield, King and Hung plan to expand to many more sports beyond basketball. Eddie Jim Coaches previously spent hours going through vision to manually track statistics, which were often inaccurate because of human error. Those same coaches can now upload footage to Superstat, input basic details such as player numbers, names and jersey colours for AI tagging purposes – and the app does the rest. At the end of the process, users receive an NBA-like box score, including points, rebounds, assists, turnovers, and field goal and free throw attempts, as well as individual minutes played and plus/minus totals for each athlete.

Advertisement

An example of from Superstat’s AI coaching tool. Superstat Superstat also generates team and individual shot charts, and individual player highlights (and lowlights) for coaches to analyse, or parents to send to grandparents. An AI assistant coach offers suggestions on what to focus on at training, too, and answers questions on game trends. The real-life coach could ask something like: “What are my team’s strengths?“. Or, “Has my team’s free throw shooting improved?” or “Where do we need to get better?” The AI assistant coach will then provide an answer, within seconds, from the game data that is uploaded. Using AI technology in this way is a significant step for amateur and junior sport.

Advertisement

Similar basketball analytics and video platforms, such as the US-based Hoopalytics, use AI only for offerings like player evaluations and scouting reports, while still paying human analysts to track the actual statistics. “We thought that a big issue might be that no-one films the games – but everyone does,” Bloomfield said. Superstat hopes to help teams discover the next Josh Giddey. Justin McManus “We want [our app] to kind of be like Strava, with what they’ve done for running and cycling. I’ll use Strava, and it’ll tell me what my next run should be. I feel like an Olympian when I go for my 5km run at my six-minute [per kilometre] pace because I get my VO2 max, my cadence and more. “We want that for player development, and to be able to help players and tell them, ‘Here’s what you’re good at, here’s what you can work on, here’s what to do at training this week’.”

Advertisement

Related Article AFL 2026 AFL stars are being targeted by ‘AI slop’. There’s a sinister motive behind it Among Superstat’s almost 6000 active monthly users is Joe Barker, who coaches one of Collingwood’s under-12 representative teams in the Victorian Junior Basketball League. “What I really like is that it highlights the ‘unsung’ parts of the game that don’t always get recognised – things like rebounds, assists, defensive effort and doing the little things that help the team,” Barker said. “It gives every player a chance to see where they’re contributing, while also giving me useful information to shape training and help the kids improve week to week.” Going beyond the box score

Advertisement

King loves that their app could play a role in recruiting decisions shifting from subjective to objective decisions based on detailed game data. It is part of the vision for the Superstat crew. They have already held discussions with US colleges such as Arizona State, who employ an Australian among their scouting staff. An example of the data generated by the Superstat app. Adobe Stock/supplied Like most sporting organisations, Arizona State have a budget that restricts their recruiting pool to areas they can send scouts to – but Superstat’s AI modelling could change the game in that sense. “The recruitment system in the US is still quite archaic,” King said.

Advertisement

“A lot of it is literally sending YouTube highlights to colleges, and you’ve got to be amazing in the first 30 seconds [to attract attention]. You send a cold email, or DM [direct message], and hopefully, someone sees it. Anything we can do to improve that visibility is a bonus.” Two of Australia’s preeminent experts in AI and sport, Dr Machar Reid and Dr Sam Robertson, don’t believe recruiters have anything to worry about in the foreseeable future. Robertson, who consults for elite sporting organisations and clubs in the US, Europe and Australia on innovation, said AI tagging, which Superstat uses, and its efficiency benefits were this technology’s best use so far. Could AI help sports recruiters better identify the best young talents, such as Richmond’s Sam Lalor? Getty Images However, Robertson was not convinced, at least yet, that AI could positively impact the talent identification process.

Advertisement

Reid, Tennis Australia’s director of innovation, was more optimistic, but agreed with Robertson that using AI to help unearth future stars was “infinitely more complex than just tagging a game”. “The application of AI to talent ID is likely easier and more effective in sports like swimming, tennis, and maybe even golf. So the individual pursuits,” Reid said. “You have a single competitor, perhaps a single technical action to analyse ... there are fewer variables that exist outside your control. From a modelling point of view, the exercise is simpler. “That doesn’t mean it will solve all your dilemmas … but team sports will take a while longer, if indeed they ever get there. You’re always going to, I think, have the human there and that element of heuristics that are important.” That reality has not stopped Superstat’s founders from thinking big.

Advertisement

They hope to take advantage of AI’s rapidly increasing sophistication to one day be able to analyse and measure an athlete’s performance more closely to offer even greater insights. Related Article AI Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg writes 6500-word essay on the future “What we’re looking to build isn’t just a system that’s good on a box score level, but more of a visual level,” chief technology officer Hung said. “We want to be able to identify, ‘If this person’s this tall, and he’s playing in this age group, he should be doing better, or moving this way to perform even better, or help the team in this way’. That’s another layer of data that we’re trying to get to.” Come back next weekend for the second part of this masthead’s series on how AI is changing sport. title: Investor home loans nose dive as they retreat from market
text:

The number of home loans taken out by investors has slumped by almost 9 per cent, new data has revealed. But the figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics reveal the drop is concentrated among investors looking to buy an existing home, with loans for the construction of new properties actually increasing. Investor loans for new construction actually rose, but the number of overall investor loans was down almost 9 per cent. Joe Armao The bureau reported that all loans fell by 5.4 per cent in the June quarter to be just 0.1 per cent up over the past 12 months. Among investors, the fall was 8.6 per cent. Since the start of the year, investor home loans have fallen by 12.9 per cent.

Advertisement

The largest drop has been among loans taken out by investors for an existing property. These fell by 14.8 per cent in the quarter during which the federal government announced its changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The negative gearing change excludes investors who borrow to build a new property. That seems to be having an impact. Loans to investors for a new home grew by 4.4 per cent and hit an all-time high for data that only goes back to 2019. Loading The bureau’s head of finance statistics, Mish Tan, noted that loans taken out by all borrower types had fallen over the past three months.

Advertisement

“Lending conditions continued to change in the June quarter, with the Reserve Bank increasing the cash rate for the third time in 2026. Changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were also announced in the federal budget in May, to commence in July 2027,” she said. Tan noted there was a substantial fall in loans taken out by investors. “The fall in investor loans in the June quarter was the largest fall since September quarter 2022,” she said. “Annually, growth in investor loans slowed from 19.4 per cent in the March quarter to 2.8 per cent this quarter.” The largest drop in investor loans was in NSW, down by 15.5 per cent, while they tumbled by 14.2 per cent in Victoria and by 10.1 per cent in Queensland.

But it is not a national story. Investor loans increased by 12.8 per cent in the Northern Territory, by 8.7 per cent in the ACT and by 5.3 per cent in Tasmania. Related Article Opinion

Australian economy Feeling miserable? The soft market meant average mortgage sizes eased, with the national average mortgage falling to $731,000 from $735,000. It is still almost 7.8 per cent up over the past year. NSW’s average mortgage dropped to $842,000 from $861,000, but remains well above the $815,000 recorded in June last year. title: How a 1990s radio quiz helped the Wallabies celebrate their 1000th player

Sometime on Saturday evening in Townsville, Massimo De Lutiis will be presented with a Test cap in the Wallabies’ dressing room. Like cricket’s Baggy Green, the old-style cap will be green, with gold trim, and the number “1000” will be embroidered on the side. That will be De Lutiis’ Wallaby number (pending his almost-certain entry into the game from the bench), and the presentation will be made by Rugby Australia president – and Wallaby No. 774 – Nathan Sharpe. RA boss Phil Waugh, Wallaby No. 766, will also be in the room. Soon-to-be Wallabies player No. 1000, Massimo de Lutiis, and other Wallaby “centurions” who preceeded him. Graphic: Stephen Kiprillis/Images: Rugby Australia It will be a special moment for De Lutiis, a Gold Coast-raised prop with Italian and Irish heritage. But the debut of the 1000th man to play in a Test for Australia in rugby union will also provide a moment for reflection for all other Wallabies, past and present. “It gives you a perspective of how special it is to be one of the 1000,” Wallabies prop Angus Bell said this week.

Advertisement

Paddy Carew (pictured in 1899) is officially recognised as Wallaby No. 1. Rugby Australia archive What is less appreciated, though, is how we even know De Lutiis will be Wallaby No. 1000, and that Paddy Carew was No. 1, and where Sharpe, Waugh and 996 other players also sit on that list. It turns out this knowledge owes to a Sydney stockbroker who was stumped on a radio quiz show in the early 1990s. Matthew Alvarez has been Rugby Australia’s honorary statistician for a long time, but 33 years ago, he was a sports nut competing in a team on Tracey Holmes’ sports trivia quiz on ABC Grandstand radio. “We got asked a question about who was Australia’s most capped front-row forward,” Alvarez recalls. “At the time, I didn’t know, and I didn’t know where to find the answer. And it was not easy to find. But that triggered the journey.”

Advertisement

For the record, the answer (then) was Andy McIntyre; now it is James Slipper. But the murkiness of the Wallabies’ historical record launched Alvarez on a mission. He set out to produce a definitive list of all Wallabies players, in exact order, from the first Test in 1899, containing debut dates, game stats and as much biographical detail as possible. It would take him a decade to complete. “The difficult thing was being sure enough of the history for the first 100 years to not get to a point where I’d miss somebody, and therefore every other number was wrong,” Alvarez said. Matthew Alvarez, the honorary statistician of Rugby Australia, pictured in Sydney. Steven Siewart

Advertisement

Alvarez trawled through published books and yearbooks on the topic, but finding errors, he painstakingly cross-referenced every Test with available information in libraries, newspaper archives, videos and other historical records. “It was going back through to ensure we had all replacements, and anyone who was capped, and then to go through in an orderly manner and number them from the start, as per what had been done with Australian cricket, whereby they started alphabetically,” Alvarez said. “Their game had been going before ours, so that was a simple benchmark to then number ours accordingly, rather than trying to give it to whoever was wearing jersey No. 1. That was too complicated, because jersey numbering has changed significantly over the years.” Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Wallaby No. 988, after his first cap at Twickenham in 2024. Julius Dimitaga/Rugby Australia So Carew was designated Wallaby No. 1, out of all the players in the first side in 1899 which beat the British Isles 13-3 at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Advertisement

“It took almost 10 good years from the time I started to get to the point where I was comfortable putting the numbers to everyone,” Alvarez said. The complete Wallaby list was first published in Inside Rugby magazine in 2002 (with Dan Vickerman the most recent Wallaby at the time, No. 777). It was later embraced by the Australian Rugby Union as the official list. All the Wallaby player numbers for new players – and retrospectively to those who’d come before – are based on Alvarez’s master document. Vic Richards, Wallaby No. 300, playing for Randwick in 1935. Sydney Morning Herald Archive The rules were (and are) simple: you become a capped Wallaby when you run on the field in a Test, and your number is based on alphabetical order if you run on at the same time as another debutant, be it in a starting XV or in a group of substitutes. Figuring out the order of substitutes was sometimes tricky, particularly for those games with limited records and/or video. Wallaby numbers are now entrenched in the game, and are referenced heavily by the Wallabies and the Classic Wallabies. They are cherished by players, a number of whom have tattoos, safely due to Alvarez’s diligence.

Advertisement

But most have no idea that the Wallaby number concept is relatively new. That includes former Test centre Adam Ashley-Cooper, who is a former milestone man as Wallaby No. 800. The “centurions” provide a nice snapshot of Wallabies history, and four are living: Chris “Buddha” Handy was 600 in 1978, Peter Jorgensen (700 in 1992), Ashley-Cooper and Sefa Naivalu (900 in 2017). Ashley-Cooper’s manic debut in 2005 is almost folklore. The young centre from the NSW Central Coast was travelling with the Wallabies as a development player when he was named as an emergency reserve for a Test against South Africa in Perth.

Advertisement

When Elton Flatley lost vision in the warm-up, Ashley-Cooper (AAC) was rushed out of the stands to get a jersey and boots and join the bench. The after-dinner story goes that AAC had downed a pie and a beer already, and he adds another pie and beer with each telling. Adam Ashley-Cooper on debut in 2005. Getty Images Wearing a jersey without a number, he became Wallaby No. 800 with a few minutes on the field at the end of the Test, when Clyde Rathbone went down with a “cork”. “That was the code among players back in the day,” Ashley-Cooper said. “You did what you could to get a debutant on. I did the same for two blokes later on in my career: Ben Tapuai and Pat McCabe.” Ashley-Cooper had to borrow the suit of assistant coach Scott Wisemantel to receive his Test cap post-match.

Advertisement

“I was thinking, ‘What the f--- just happened?’ – it was such a whirlwind,” he said. Ashley-Cooper’s debut even became a trivia question on a Tooheys bottle cap, which his father Tony proudly showed him a few years later. Who is the only Wallaby to debut without a number on his back? “He goes, ‘You’ve made it’, and I’m like, “Mate, I’ve played over 50 games for the Wallabies’, and he says, ‘This is my proudest moment!’,” Ashley-Cooper says with a laugh. Ashley-Cooper played 121 Tests for the Wallabies, a rarity for all the centurion milestone men. Most only played a handful.

Advertisement

But that, too, is consistent with Alvarez’s data. The average Test tally for a Wallaby over 127 years is 13 Tests, and even that’s been inflated by an explosion of Tests in the professional era. Before 1996, the average was eight Tests. Related Article Updated

Australian rugby Kiss flags big change to Wallabies’ attack after major reshuffle for Japan rematch “More than 18 per cent of all Wallabies (185) have only played one test,” Alvarez notes. “And more than 40 per cent have played three or fewer tests.” The average career lasts for 2½ years, and the 1920s, when rugby was rebuilding after a war that took the lives of 500 Australian rugby players, was the decade with the most debutants, at 121. In 126 years and 717 Test matches, the average age of all Wallabies debutants has been 23.8.

Advertisement

De Lutiis is ahead of the curve, at 22, and his career length is yet to be determined. But one thing seems certain: you can bank on Massimo De Lutiis, Wallaby No. 1000, being the answer to a trivia question. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: Pigeons will love Clover’s $150m vision for Town Hall. We might prefer a food court
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWSydney Opinion Pigeons will love Clover’s $150m vision for Town Hall. We might prefer a food court Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist August 14, 2026 — 11:30am

August 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Like Clover Moore, we all love a square, or at least the idea of one. The City of Sydney has just unleashed its plans for a big beautiful square in front of Sydney Town Hall, the fruit of a 40-year plan to replace the existing buildings around the intersection of George, Park and Druitt streets with our own Piazza San Marco. The $150 million budget has been criticised, but the council says it has long factored this into its plan and points to the re-pedestrianising of George Street as a model of economic cost-benefit. The design for the 4500-square metre square, with 30 trees, “an interactive water feature” and fixed and movable chairs, expresses the council’s vision: “Like other great global cities, Sydney needs well-designed public spaces where people can come together, spend time and connect. A civic heart belongs to everyone – a welcoming place where everyday moments and civic life sit side by side.” An artist’s impression of the proposed square opposite Sydney Town Hall. Choi Render The Lord Mayor, Clover Moore, who has dedicated much of her 21-year tenure to increasing shared public spaces, says, “All the people now living in the city will enjoy it very much. It’ll be a Trafalgar Square, a Piccadilly Square, like Piazza San Marco in Venice.” The new square will open up views of some of the city’s historic buildings such as Sydney Town Hall, St Andrews

Cathedral and the Queen Victoria Building (and, um, the Citigroup and Ausgrid towers). Ah, the idea of a square. Old nonnas gossiping over a coffee in the morning, kids chasing balls during the day, open-air aperitifs in the twilight. In Europe, which the lord mayor likes to reference, the culture of town squares is a direct rebuttal to the Donald Trump-JD Vance lecture series on a continent “going to hell”. (If they want to see a culture going to hell, have they tried visiting the USA?)

Advertisement

But then, you might also wonder when our own visionaries last visited Europe and Britain. Trafalgar Square is a nasty roundabout jammed with open-top tourist buses and menaced by a ring of Pret A Mangers and Caffe Neros. It compares unfavourably with Trafalgar Square in Marsfield, which at least has ample parking and a bottle shop. “Piccadilly Square” is not a thing, but Piccadilly Circus is another commuter hellscape where people have to wear their mobile phones on wires around their necks while photographing the Eros statue to stop them being stolen. And Piazza San Marco might have been the “drawing room of Europe” when Napoleon was there 220 years ago, but today if you want to escape getting caught up in a group trailing after a flag, your only option is to flee into a queue for a $12 espresso. Related Article Exclusive

City life First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square Only in our dreams is the big European city square what we want it to be. In Paris and Rome, the Notre Dame and Louvre forecourts and St Peter’s Square are congested, configured around metal barricades, places you go to obey police and stand in lines. Istanbul’s Taksim Square is an intersection, and in Florence’s Piazza della Signoria you can watch the world go by in the guise of monstrous facial surgeries, American nepo babies and Ferragamo bags. The ideal European squares are not the famous ones; they’re the small ones in big towns or the big ones in small towns. In square-filled cities like Madrid, Bologna and Brussels, the main square is the crappiest one, the retail and restaurant culture blighted by extortionate rents and overtourism. The squares that still manage to embody our ideals are the little out-of-the-way ones, with old cafes and bars and communities centred usually around churches, where competition does not dictate behaviour and where you can be as contented-looking as the folk in the City of Sydney’s artists’ impressions of its new square. It’s a dream, but it’s not in the middle of the big city and it’s contained in complex cultural traditions rather than utopian social engineering. Which brings me to my point, which is that a town square is cultural more than physical. Small squares based around the way people live in apartment cities, “where people come together, spend time and connect”, have emerged organically over time. A big square can’t magically invent those customs: at best, it can only express what is already in the culture. The new square, says the lord mayor, isn’t going to try to copy the European ones; it’s “going to be very Sydney and it’s going to be very Australian”.

Advertisement

But what does that mean? How do Sydney’s built public spaces express who we are? Pedestrian malls like the Manly Corso, Oxford Street Mall in Bondi Junction and Parramatta Square hardly bring to life the vision splendid. Stepping out of the way of oncoming ebikes and wiping the bird poo off the public seats, our mall life is hobbled by the Australian disease of high rents and short-term retail tenancies. In 20 years, our summertime climate will have turned concrete outdoor squares into no-go zones. Trafalgar Square’s water fountains were fenced off this week amid 36C temperatures during the fifth heatwave to hit England this European summer. Getty Images If the City of Sydney wanted to study how we actually use public spaces, it might look out the window. A pebblecrete wasteland, home to the homeless, Town Hall Square could be Sussan Ley’s next project when she wants to see how the Australian other half lives. Town Hall Square belongs to that 20th-century utopian planning notion that if you build an open space you will change people’s behaviour; architecture can create community. In Town Hall Square, architecture has created a community for pigeons and a small quota of allowable protesters, largely a place people rush through as if avoiding sniper fire. Finally admitting defeat on Town Hall Square, the council is to refurbish it next year as “Sydney Square”, a new experiment to see if removing pebblecrete and changing a name can re-engineer the way we live. As much as we would like to see the $150 million square, which will have a “Sydney Aboriginal” name, realise the council’s 40-year vision, it’s also possible that Sydney people just don’t do public squares. We do Westfields and food courts, we do parks and green spaces (sometimes), we do sports grounds and fish markets, but throughout the Sydney suburbs our built public spaces are often dispiritingly windswept and avoidable, a disappointment to the dreams of those who planned them.

Advertisement

The City of Sydney envisions “a lively gathering place for generations to come”. In its artists’ impressions of the new square, those generations walk, talk and smile, or (Clover Moore’s words) sit as they already do on George Street “on those seats every day under the trees, looking at the flowers, chatting to their friends”. In the drawings, not a single one is doing what Sydney people actually do, which is rush somewhere else, scarf takeaway while wearing earpods, or sit in a Talmudic hunch over their phones, living their lives in the virtual town square, the only one they know. Do we want public squares – or food courts? Cole Bennetts Nobody in the artists’ picture is squabbling over a table, nobody is dealing with a previous occupant’s rubbish, and nobody is staring blank-eyed at the overpriced coffee and muffin they have just been forced to acquire from the chain eateries which are the only ones that can afford the surrounding rents. It’s hardly the Europhile vision, but here we go, we’re optimists, always ready to give ourselves another try. Malcolm Knox is a journalist, author and columnist. title: Disney diehards take their fandom to infinity, and beyond
text:
