By the time you’re reading this, tens of thousands of Disney fans will be pushing through the turnstiles at the studio’s D23 convention in Anaheim, California, the House of Mouse spin-off to San Diego Comic-Con which draws Disney diehards from around the world. They have come to meet the stars of Disney projects, see and hear first-look trailers and announcements, and buy toys. Lots and lots of toys. D23, a one-stop shop which merges branded marketing and old-school fan convention, is as renowned for its cosplaying fans as it is for the nearby Honda Stadium showcases, which will, over this weekend, unveil the next two years of Disney’s plans in the realms of streaming TV, animated and live-action movies, and theme park and cruise attractions. Think of them as Hillsong for plush toys and roller coasters. Happy clappers? Disney fans worshipping at the altar of the House of Mouse in 2024. So, what is likely to lead the headlines? The most anticipated drop is likely to be either a teaser trailer or a glimpse of production footage from Star Wars: Starfighter. The film, produced by Disney-owned Lucasfilm and set five years after the events of Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker, will star Ryan Gosling and is expected in cinemas in 2027. That makes this year’s D23 the most likely staging ground to start marketing it to Disney-brand diehards. A year out from release and so far, not a single frame marketed to the audience? That’s an oversight. Expect it to be corrected. Directed by Shawn Levy and written by Jonathan Tropper, the film also has an intriguing supporting cast: Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Aaron Pierre and Amy Adams among them.

Advertisement

Marvel’s big ticket announcement is likely to be X-Men related, specifically the upcoming reboot directed by Jake Schreier. What makes that significant? Schreier’s last film Thunderbolts was a refreshing spin on the Marvel universe, which is beginning to show its age in story and casting terms. Gift with purchase: it’s written by Lee Sung Jin (Beef) and Joanna Calo (The Bear). Two buzzier writers you will not find. On the X-Men front, there is already persistent online chatter. Sadie Sink is tipped to play telepathic and telekinetic Jean Grey, Kit Connors has been tipped to play Cyclops and Samara Weaving is tipped to play diamond-hard super heroine Emma Frost. Marvel’s Kevin Feige is expected to confirm those castings, and unveil more. But there’s less urgency here; the X-Men reboot is not due in cinemas until late 2028. Feeling the call of the Force: Star Wars fans at a “cosplay meetup” at D23. The Disney animation headliner will almost certainly be Hexed, the studio’s upcoming supernatural coming-of-age film about a young witch discovering her powers. Disney unveiled the voice cast and a glimpse of the film at the CinemaCon convention in Las Vegas. Audiences at D23 are expected to be given an extensive preview of the film. But rumours suggest Disney is also likely to tap its legacy well, with news about a third instalment of the Frozen franchise. Late 2027 is the date earmarked for the film, and this year’s D23 is a critical step; D23 only happens every other year, and next year’s marketing calendar will be dominated by the 50th anniversary of Star Wars.

Advertisement

Disney is expected to showcase a couple of other Lucasfilm and Marvel titles. The second season of the Star Wars series Ahsoka is long overdue, and a new trailer is likely to drop. The second season is due early in 2027, and in a highly competitive space like D23 (and it’s non-Disney cousin, San Diego Comic-Con) buzz doesn’t come cheap. Marvel is also expected to drop footage from this year’s Avengers: Doomsday. With a December release date, that film might as well be opening next week for the time left to ramp the marketing noise up a notch. And critically, coming off big box office returns for The Odyssey, Moana and Spider-Man, “nobody goes to the movies” is wearing thin as an excuse for underperforming films. Rosario Dawson as Ahsoka Tano. The show’s second season is expected to be among this year’s big reveals. Lucasfilm Though the convention is pitched wider than the company’s streaming assets, all roads lead ultimately to an arms race in the digital television space. Disney’s core asset is threefold: Disney+, the US-based Hulu and ESPN+ which command, between them, a paid subscriber base of around 207 million people worldwide. The market leader, and logically Disney’s major competitor, Netflix, has more than 325 million subscribers worldwide. That looks like a commanding margin, however, Netflix’s core assets lack the pop culture appeal of Disney’s. Marvel and Star Wars are, after all, hard to argue with.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks While major announcements will make headlines in the mainstream media, D23 also feeds a raft of very detailed reveals to a micro-economy of Disney-focused news websites and blogs, YouTube channels and fan podcasts, with names like All Ears, Blog Mickey and Mice Chat, which unpack content announcements and theme park developments in minute detail. The dozen or so most-read of those sites generate as many as 100 million page views on a busy month, with more than 120 million subscribers to major social video channels across YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. If measured as a single consolidated vertical, that micro-economy is worth more than US$300 million. Of particular interest to those sites will be the company’s plans for new theme park extensions, including Villain’s Land, the most substantial addition to a Disney parks since the launch the Star Wars-themed Galaxy’s Edge in 2019. Villain’s Land, at Walt Disney World in Florida, will be themed entirely around the villains of Disney stories, including Maleficent (Sleeping Beauty), Ursula (The Little Mermaid) and Jafar (Aladdin). D23 is held every other year in Anaheim, California. The event draws as many as 100,000 people through its gates across a three-day weekend, excluding a separate D23 Disneyland day and, this year, a D23-branded baseball match at Dodger Stadium. The injection of revenue into the local economy, including accommodation, dining, transport and retail is worth an estimated US$55 million.

title: For Geelong, the safest path on Kolodjashnij was the hardest. They took the easy way
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion For Geelong, the safest path on Kolodjashnij was the hardest. They took the easy way Darren Kane Sports Columnist August 14, 2026 — 11:30am

August 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Everyone walking upright has this week opined on the vexed matter of Jake Kolodjashnij and his treatment by his employer, the Geelong Football Club. To recap, Kolodjashnij, a 30-year-old player with a history of concussive incidents, signed a waiver that saw him assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries in a secret deal with the Cats that was not approved by the AFL. Loading The latest development, of the AFL Commission instructing an independent lawyer to determine whether the clubhas contravened any AFL rule, is important. It’s equally irrespective. Kolodjashnij’s injury history was in 2024 examined by the AFL’s concussion panel, which effectively green-lighted him to continue playing. That isn’t the same as being given an entirely clean bill of health. These things can be inconclusive and not sufficient to end a player’s career, but at the same time problematic.

Advertisement

What seems to have occurred next, though, is perplexing. In circumstances where AFL players are excluded from statutory worker’s compensation schemes, and where it’s vanishingly impossible for them to secure alternate coverage in the insurance marketplace that includes cover for head trauma and latent-onset neurological conditions, the Cats asked the player to execute a document as a condition of continued employment. A document which apparently included provisions regarding Kolodjashnij’s informed consent (ie, an acknowledgement of what he would be exposing himself to by continuing to play) and what has been portrayed as a “liability waiver”, purported to exonerate the club. Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij. Getty This document – also, apparently – was produced under a cloak of secrecy, to the point it wasn’t disclosed to the AFL Players Association nor registered with the AFL. To me, that’s troubling stuff.If Geelong felt it had nothing to fear, why did its guiding minds think it had anything to hide? If it’s true that there’s a chain of email correspondence between the AFL and the club about the concept and development of this document, then that’s relevant evidence but doesn’t free anyone from blame. Sporting rules are one thing, but one thing only.

Advertisement

The better focus is on asking what was going on inside the minds of those who signed off on this arrangement. The Geelong Football Club is a company. The Corporations Act requires that directors and officers of companies exercise their powers and discharge their duties with the degree of care and diligence a reasonable person would if they were a director or officer of a company in the same circumstances. Legislation is, of course, for the courts to interpret. The test is not whether the directors did the right thing: Instead, it’s a question of was the decision, viewed prospectively, one that a reasonably careful director could make having regard to the risks and potential benefits? On one side of the ledger is the prospect of continued services being provided by an experienced and, evidently, excellent footballer. On the other side sit the risks of brain injuries being sustained by an uninsurable player, and the associated risks and harm that might flow. If what Kolodjashnij signed does incorporate words amounting to a “waiver”, in my experience clients don’t routinely instruct lawyers to draft special contractual waivers for risks never foreseen. The concealment of the waiver from the AFL and AFLPA – whether by deceitful intention, or a systems failure– strains the notion of any of this being implemented in good faith and for a proper purpose. Again, if you’ve nothing to fear you’ve nothing to hide. Further, the Corporations Act also requires directors and officers more generally to exercise their powers and discharge their duties in good faith, for a proper purpose and in the best interests of the company. In the context of a professional sporting franchise, these “best interests” extend beyond filling shelves of a trophy cabinet. Consider its covenant with its 90,000-odd members, and its duty of candour.

Advertisement

Ask yourself again – is it in good faith and proper, for Geelong’s directors and senior management to have proceeded down this path? Knowing the apparent risks to which the player would be exposed? Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 Kolodjashnij told me about his ‘tough conversations’. His case reveals much bigger issues Moreover, did those guiding minds turn to the question of whether this clandestine arrangement had any legal force? AFL standard playing contracts, buttressed by the collective bargaining agreement, do not permit “side deals” as to the reapportionment of legal liability. The contracting arrangements certainly don’t countenance the idea of secret deals. It’s hardly certain this document would be enforceable. Moreover, a release signed in 2024 doesn’t easily swallow a neurodegenerative disease manifesting in 2046, absent the clearest imaginable words. Aside from any other factor, how could one satisfactorily demonstrate that what Kolodjashnij was exposed to before executing the document did not matter? Further, it’s express under the CBA that AFL clubs provide and maintain safe working environments for players as far as is reasonably practicable. That’s consistent with the Victorian statutory position under the Occupational Health and Safety Act.

Advertisement

The words “reasonably practicable” constitute a defined calculus. This refers to the likelihood of the hazard, the degree of harm, what the employer knows or ought to know, and the availability and cost of controls. What’s absent is the matter of the employee’s consent. These workplace duties are criminal in character, owed by the employer to the state and prosecuted by the regulator. The duties aren’t in the nature of private rights a footballer can bargain away, which is why a signed release isn’t an answer to any prosecution. The OH&S Act asks whether the risk was eliminated or reduced, where a “waiver” achieves neither, and instead is a liability instrument masquerading as something else. Overall, though, the best question here that directors should ask, is not merely can we do this, but should we? For the law of directors’ duties sets a floor, not a licence. And here’s where the analysis ceases being merely legal, because duties were never designed as a ceiling on conscience. The genuinely hard decisions in any boardroom aren’t choices between right and wrong; they’re choices between defensible and right. It strikes me that Geelong’s board had three roads to choose to roll down. The easy road, which it seemingly did. The middle road, of disclosing this special arrangement to the AFL and the AFLPA, and letting the sun shine on it. Or the hard road, of sitting with Jake Kolodjashnij, his manager and his family, and having the difficult, career-ending and tear-stained conversation.

Advertisement

The perverse elegance here, is that the hardest road was simultaneously the safest one to traverse; legally, ethically and reputationally. The concept of courage appears nowhere in the Corporations Act, yet it’s the substrate on which every duty in the legislation depends – because a director who can’t say the hardest word has outsourced the job to whoever can. None of this is a charge against Kolodjashnij; nor entirely against the individuals on Geelong’s board, several of whom are experienced, decent directors – who I suspect know precisely how this looks. Rather, it’s a charge against a system that abandons clubs and players in a room with an uninsurable risk; and against a boardroom culture that mistook a defensible YES for quite possibly a contrary, correct answer.

title: A third Sydney airport runway incident under investigation
text:
in brief A Virgin flight had its takeoff cancelled after a Qantas plane crossed its path on the runway.

ATSB has launched a safety investigation into the incident.

Australia's transport safety watchdog has launched an investigation into a third near-collision incident between two planes at Sydney airport in as many weeks.

The potential collision happened just hours after a similar incident last week made national and international headlines and sparked widespread safety concerns. A crew member was injured in that incident.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau announced on Thursday night that it had opened an investigation into the runway incursion involving two Boeing 737 jets at 10am on 9 August.

"The incident occurred when a Virgin Australia 737 was cleared by air traffic control (ATC) for take-off from Sydney’s runway 34L," the ATSB said in a statement to SBS News.

"As the crew applied thrust for take-off, they observed a Qantas 737 crossing the runway ahead of them on taxiway Lima.

"The Qantas crew reported they had been cleared by ATC to cross the runway.

"Upon seeing the Qantas aircraft, the Virgin Australia crew reduced thrust and the aircraft came to a stop, roughly a kilometre from the intersection."

The Qantas jet crossed the takeoff path of the Virgin flight, forcing ATC to cancel the latter's departure clearance "at the same time".

The ATSB said investigations were already underway, with evidence being gathered and interviews with the involved parties expected to be conducted.

Footage of the Jetstar-Qatar incident was captured and shared on social media on Sunday. Source: Supplied / @itsdanibrown / X

On Sunday, a Jetstar flight had to slam on the brakes to avoid hitting a Qatar Airways plane being towed across the tarmac.

The two weekend incidents come just weeks after two Qantas flights, with ATC permission, managed to narrowly avoid contact in Sydney at the end of July.

All three incidents are under investigation by the national transport safety watchdog, which operates "no fault" fact-finding missions in order to prevent similar incidents from occurring, rather than to take punitive action.

On Monday, ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said that the Jetstar-Qatar incident "could have been far more serious" and that incidents like that "shouldn't happen".

"We do have an aviation sector that is the envy of the world. That's not to say that with incidents like this, we don't take them seriously to improve," he said.

"But aircraft movements, whether it be in a busy airport or in the skies, are incredibly well coordinated here in Australia."

Airservices Australia — the government-owned corporation responsible for managing air traffic control across much of the country — admitted on Monday that it had been too reliant on overtime staffing hours.

Last weekend, hundreds of flights from Sydney were delayed after air traffic control workers called in sick.

Air traffic work is both demanding and needed 365 days a year. Experts have told SBS News that a high-performing air-traffic controller takes around five years to build up sufficient skills and experience.

Federal Transport Minister Catherine King said emergency meetings were held in Canberra on Monday following the disruptions to air travel but said she was "confident" that Airservices Australia was doing "everything they can to get on top of this".

title: The fertility flaw in men's testosterone obsession
text:
The internet's obsession with "maxxing" has turned almost every aspect of self-improvement into a trend.

Young men now swap tips on optimising everything from sleep and appearance to testosterone, longevity and mental performance.

Male fertility has increasingly been drawn into that world, too. Social media is awash with advice ranging from sensible lifestyle changes to more questionable suggestions, such as icing the testicles, eating raw garlic and taking long lists of supplements.

Saunas and ice bath "cold plunges" have become especially popular, promoted as ways to boost testosterone, improve sperm health and increase the chances of conception.

But how much of this advice is actually supported by evidence? And could some of these popular wellness practices have the opposite effect to the one intended?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Where hype meets evidence

One of the biggest misconceptions behind many of these claims is that testosterone and fertility are essentially the same thing. They aren't.

Testosterone is essential for normal male reproductive function. However, higher blood testosterone — as many online wellness claims promise — does not automatically produce healthier sperm or improve the likelihood of conception.

In fact, taking testosterone can suppress sperm production. The American Urological Association and American Society for Reproductive Medicine advise against testosterone therapy for men interested in current or future fertility.

The distinction between testosterone and fertility is also important when it comes to saunas and cold plunges, which are often touted to benefit both.

Saunas or cold plunges may indeed improve sleep, reduce stress or support general wellbeing. But those benefits should not be confused with evidence of improved fertility.

The more important question is whether heat or cold actually affects sperm quality and the likelihood of conception.

Why? Because the testes sit outside the body for a reason: sperm production works best below core body temperature.

A large 2024 study followed more than 15,000 Chinese men and analysed over 28,000 semen samples.

Exposure to extreme temperatures was associated with poorer semen quality, including lower sperm concentration, total count and motility. While hot weather and sauna use are clearly different, the findings support broader evidence that heat can disrupt sperm production.

Perhaps the strongest evidence on saunas comes from an Italian longitudinal study, in which ten healthy men completed two 15-minute Finnish sauna sessions each week at 80-90C for three months.

Their sperm count and motility declined, alongside changes in mitochondrial function and sperm DNA packaging. Reassuringly, these changes had reversed six months after they stopped using the sauna.

Another United States-led study followed couples trying to conceive. Hot baths and hot tubs alone had little effect on pregnancy rates. But men with greater cumulative exposure to multiple heat sources had moderately lower chances of conception.

If heat can impair sperm production, it might be assumed that cold exposure must improve fertility. Current evidence doesn't support that conclusion.

A systematic review by Australian researchers found cold-water immersion may reduce muscle soreness and aid short-term recovery after strenuous exercise. Another Australian-led 2025 review also reported possible benefits for stress, sleep and quality of life.

Although the evidence was limited by small studies and inconsistent methods, neither review found evidence that cold-water immersion improves testosterone, sperm quality or pregnancy rates.

Targeted scrotal cooling has been investigated as a treatment for male infertility, but that is very different from immersing the whole body in cold water. Nor is there evidence that applying ice after a sauna reverses the effects of heat exposure.

So, while cold plunges may help recovery after exercise, they shouldn't be viewed or promoted as a fertility hack.

What about women?

Wellness claims about optimising female fertility are also widespread, although they are usually framed around "hormone balance", "egg quality" or fertility optimisation rather than the male-oriented world of maxxing.

The scientific evidence, however, is much less developed. A 2024 systematic review by US researchers found the reproductive effects of heat remain underexplored, with little evidence from human studies.

Likewise, research on cold exposure and female reproductive function is largely based on animal studies, meaning we still do not know whether cold-water immersion affects ovulation, egg quality or conception in women.

Pregnancy raises separate questions, so anyone who is pregnant, or has concerns about their reproductive health, should seek advice from an appropriately qualified health professional.

But for most healthy adults, an occasional sauna or cold plunge is unlikely to determine whether they can have children.

As with many wellness trends, the problem isn’t necessarily the practice itself. It’s the tendency to assume one claimed benefit automatically leads to another.

A sauna may support relaxation or sleep. A cold plunge may aid alertness and exercise recovery.

But piling one wellness trend on top of another, without evidence to support it, doesn't necessarily improve health. And in some cases, particularly when it comes to fertility, people may only be "maxxing" what they least intend to.

Hoani Smith is a lecturer in sport management and sport science at Lincoln University, New Zealand. Conrad Goodhew is an assistant lecturer at the School of Health Sciences at the University of Canterbury. title: A decade longer, $275,000 dearer: The trade-off facing Aussie home buyers
text:
In brief A number of Australian lenders now offer 40-year mortgages.

Canstar's Sally Tindall said it's far from the answer to Australia's housing affordability problem.

Imagine paying a mortgage from today until 2066. For some Australians, that could become a reality as more lenders offer 40-year home loans.

In the last few years, an increasing number of smaller lenders in Australia have begun to offer these extended loan terms — a decade longer than the standard 30-year term.

Australian bank AMP was the latest to jump on the bandwagon, recently announcing a new 40-year mortgage product for investors.

It joins a relatively small list of competitors including Credit Union SA, Unity Bank, Great Southern Bank, RACQ Bank, Bank of Us, Liberty and Pepper Money.

Sally Tindall, data insights director at financial comparison site Canstar, told SBS News many of the 40-year mortgages are geared towards younger people and first-home buyers.

Last year, a Finder survey found that 30 per cent of Australians would take out a 40-year mortgage if it reduced their monthly repayments to a more affordable level.

But experts warn there are major downsides that would-be borrowers should weigh.

The trade-offs of a 40-year mortgage

With house prices at historic highs, a longer loan term can make it easier for some Australians to enter the housing market by reducing monthly repayments, improving their serviceability or increasing how much they can borrow.

But it comes at significant cost.

According to an analysis by Canstar, an additional decade of repayments on a $600,000 mortgage could reduce a borrower's initial monthly repayments by around $288 but result in nearly $275,000 in extra interest over the life of the loan.

"It improves someone's chances of getting the green light on a loan that they might not have otherwise been able to afford," Tindall told SBS News.

"But really, if you are someone that is struggling to pay off a debt over 30 years, it's worth stopping and thinking, well, is the size of the amount I want to borrow too high for my financial situation?"

Last year, when Great Southern Bank introduced a new 40-year loan, its chief customer officer, Rolf Stromsoe, suggested the product could be a stepping stone for first-home buyers, allowing them to enter the market before ultimately refinancing.

"As their needs evolve and their earnings capacity changes, they may refinance any number of times — but this is the loan that can start it all," he said.

But Tindall warned that refinancing may be a challenge with this type of product, given the limited pool of lenders that offer them and their high-risk profile.

It also exposes borrowers to the risk of being trapped in a loan they could struggle to refinance.

"Is that pay rise guaranteed? Is that promotion guaranteed? Absolutely not," Tindall asked.

"It might all work out fantastically. It might not, and so it's really important to be looking at the alternatives, so that you understand the risks of that particular strategy, and go in with your eyes open."

She added that with fewer lenders to choose from, interest rates on these loans could be less competitive.

A growing trend?

Amid a global housing affordability crunch, longer loans are also gaining traction in several other countries.

In the UK, mortgages stretching beyond 30 years have become increasingly common, while 50-year loans are gaining popularity among younger buyers in Japan.

In the US, President Donald Trump floated the prospect of a 50-year mortgage last year.

Sarah Megginson, personal finance expert at Finder, said she expects more lenders may start offering 40-year loans in Australia as housing becomes increasingly out of reach for many buyers.

"I think that we will see more banks respond to customer demands by looking at different ways they can evolve their products and get more lending happening," she told SBS News.

And as the cost of living burden leaves households with limited wiggle room in their budgets, she said, the prospect of saving a few hundred dollars a month on a mortgage may be attractive to some.

"Long term, the pain is there, but in the short term, people are just looking to try and release a bit of pressure," she said, describing longer loan terms as offering "short-term gain for long-term pain".

Tindall, however, doesn't think there's appetite for many lenders to offer 40-year loans.

"I don't think they're going to become more common," she said. "APRA (The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority) sees them as risky, and certainly the big banks don't touch them."

The banking regulator has previously said it places greater scrutiny on higher-risk mortgage lending, which includes lending at very long terms.

There are a range of factors behind this, Tindall said, including the sheer length of the loan. Someone taking out a 40-year mortgage in their 40s could still be paying it off well into retirement, in their 80s.

She doesn't believe longer loan terms are the answer to Australia's housing affordability problem — far from it.

"I can't see a world where we move towards a 40-year mortgage as a solution to overpaying on a property."

"What we need to see in order to make housing more affordable is more stock and lower prices, rather than just getting people to sign up for longer debts."

title: Here's when the Census results will be released — and what they'll reveal
text:
in brief Results from the 2026 Census will be released across three stages.

Information is used by governments, councils, businesses, community organisations and researchers to understand Australia's changing needs.

Australians will have to wait until the middle of next year to see the first results of the 2026 Census, with the full dataset not expected until 2028.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) will release the results in three stages, starting in mid-2027 and continuing into the following year.

Jenny Telford, the ABS' general manager of the Census and population statistics, explained why it takes around 10 months to release the first batch of results.

"June 2027, it might sound like a long time away, but Australia is a really big country," she said on Thursday.

"It takes us quite a while to bring in every paper form from every part of remote Australia. Lots of work ahead of us, but June next year is when we'll release that picture of the nation."

Over eight million completed Census forms had been received by Wednesday morning, the ABS confirmed, accounting for over two-thirds of Australians.

When will the 2026 Census results be released?

The first release is scheduled for June 2027, less than a year after Census night. It will include most Census topics and cover almost all geographic areas.

This first release will provide a broad picture of Australia, including population characteristics such as age, sex recorded at birth, gender and sexual orientation.

It will also include information on family composition, relationships, country of birth, ancestry, language, religion, education, income, housing, health, disability, unpaid work and care, and other demographic characteristics.

What information will be included in each Census release?

The second release is due in October 2027.

This will add a range of employment and location-based information, including labour force status, occupation, industry, hours worked, place of work and methods of travelling to work.

This release will be particularly useful for understanding how Australia's communities function economically, including where people live and where they work. That information can help reveal commuting patterns and the links between residential areas and employment centres.

The third release is expected in early to mid-2028.

It will contain information requiring additional processing, including distance to work, estimates of homelessness and the Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA).

READ MORE What to watch out for as Census scammers go looking for victims

SEIFA provides a way to compare areas based on their relative socioeconomic characteristics and can be particularly useful for governments and organisations when identifying areas of greater need and informing decisions about funding and services.

The staged approach is designed to give the ABS time to process, check and protect the data before it is published.

What's new in the 2026 Census compared with 2021?

The 2026 Census will provide a detailed picture of how Australia has changed since 2021, from where people live and how households are structured to housing, education, employment, income and cultural background.

It will also provide new information on gender, gender experience, and sexual orientation, offering insights not available in the last Census.

Income data will also be enriched using administrative data, providing a more detailed picture of Australians' economic circumstances.

READ MORE What is new in the 2026 Census? The questions that have changed

Results will be available across a range of geographic areas, allowing users to compare changes between states, cities, suburbs, and smaller communities, and to see how Australia's population and communities have evolved since 2021.

How governments and businesses use Census data

Census information is used by governments, councils, businesses, community organisations and researchers to understand Australia's changing needs.

It helps inform decisions about schools, hospitals, housing, transport, infrastructure and local services, while businesses can use demographic and economic information to understand communities and plan investment.

title: Low-income Australians should accept substandard homes, Liberal frontbencher says
text:
in brief Liberals are this week pushing for a reduced housing code, which could streamline construction at the cost of quality.

Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg conceded that the proposal would come with "trade-offs".

The Coalition's plan to boost housing stock will involve "trade-offs", a Liberal frontbencher has said, after suggesting low-income households should accept living in substandard homes.

Opposition housing and homelessness spokesperson Andrew Bragg announced on Wednesday that the Opposition would reduce the national housing code from 2,000 pages to 80 if elected.

When asked by ABC Radio National on Thursday morning whether his policy means low-income earners should just accept living in substandard housing, he replied: "Yes, definitely."

He went on to say that building more homes under a streamlined code would come with "trade-offs".

"It's more important to have a house than to not have a house. And so, given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system, we need to just build more houses," he told the ABC.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Bragg's comments follow remarks made by his Liberal colleague and treasury spokesman Tim Wilson, who suggested in some cases people could put "a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money" on improving housing quality.

He told ABC RN on Wednesday there should not be a one-size-fits-all policy — such as mandated energy efficiency — for construction.

"There are some places in the country where you will get cold spells or hot spells for a very small amount of the year, whereas for the rest of the year, it's not necessary," he said.

"We have a risk that Australians can't afford to rent or to buy their own home by the government's own budget design. We need housing stock that meets different needs in different environmental conditions. Queensland is not the same as Tasmania or Victoria. Western Australia is different again."

Proposal does 'nothing to fix' housing crisis, advocate says

Affordable housing advocates told SBS News that stripping back construction regulations is a way for developers to profit from "unliveable" homes.

"Too many renters are already living in homes that are freezing in winter, stifling in summer, riddled with mould and damp, and expensive to heat and cool," Everybody's Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said in a statement.

"Older people and people with disability already struggle to find homes they can safely and comfortably live in."

Azize added that the government should focus on social housing that is "built to last".

"We have a housing crisis because people cannot afford a home. Building more poor-quality homes does nothing to fix that crisis. It simply gives developers another way to profit from it," Azize said.

Australian Council of Social Services CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie agreed, adding that construction of social housing should "drastically scale up".

She described Bragg's comments as shocking.

"The changes to the building code proposed by Senator Bragg would simply remove costs from the builder and move them onto the household - locking them into higher power bills for decades, deepening inequality, risking lives, leaving future generations with homes that are expensive to run," she told SBS News.

The Housing Industry Association on Wednesday welcomed Senator Bragg's announcement, but argued it was more important to disentangle layers of complexity than target a specific size of the code.

Cutting red tape

The national housing codes set minimum requirements for the safety, health, amenity, accessibility, and sustainability of certain buildings, as detailed in over 2,000 pages.

The Coalition's new standards will focus on cost-effective structural, fire safety and health-related building standards.

Bragg said reducing the code has been a shifting policy for the Coalition.

"This was in Angus Taylor's budget reply back in May, and we have committed to getting it to 200 pages, but we actually found a way to get it to less than 100 pages. It tends to be by picking up the New Zealand building code, which is about 80," he explained.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil has dismissed earlier calls to reduce construction standards to 200 pages. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

While New Zealand's building code appears to be about 80 pages long, the country has other compulsory building requirements on durability and energy efficiency, outlined in separate documents that builders must comply with.

Labor announced it would freeze the National Construction Code following its productivity roundtable in mid-2026.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil brushed off calls from the Coalition to cut the construction standards to 200 pages earlier in 2026.

"I've talked to builders about that, they laugh their heads off. That is absolutely ridiculous," O'Neil told the National Press Club in May.

The government is not far off presenting a final plan to the building minister later this year to streamline the code, Treasurer Jim Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Wednesday.

Bragg has also called for the creation of a federal pattern book of model homes that could receive automatic approval from the states and territories.

title: A melon, or a message? The prized fruit at the centre of the Albanese controversy
text:
in brief The melons gifted to Anthony Albanese by the Japanese prime minister hold cultural significance.

Albanese's discussion of the gift has prompted accusations of cultural faux pas and disrespect.

As Anthony Albanese's weeks-old comments about melons continue to fuel political drama, the fruit at the centre of the controversy has largely been overlooked.

Yet the crown melons gifted to the prime minister by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are no ordinary fruit.

In Japan, they are among the country's most prized gifts.

During an appearance on Nikki Osborne's Deep Bush podcast last month, Albanese described the melons as a "pretty strange" gift before praising their quality.

Hand gestures he made while discussing the fruit have since drawn criticism, an interpretation his office has rejected.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But what exactly did Takaichi's gift represent?

What are crown melons?

Both the fruit and gift-giving hold deep significance in Japanese culture.

Waka Ikeda, writing in the Japan Times, describes a crown melon as "perfection, based on the Japanese artisan spirit of takumi" — something you bring when you wish to honour someone. Her op-ed highlighting Albanese's comments on the podcast kickstarted the furore that has spilled over onto the international stage

Gwyn McClelland, senior lecturer in Japanese studies and president of the Japanese Studies Association of Australia, told SBS News that he shared the Japan Times story with his students to express how "incensed" he was by the prime minister's gesture.

His students were "also quite embarrassed", he said.

"I was just really annoyed that he didn't realise the giving of fruit could be really lovely and important," he said.

"In an Australian context, that doesn't look like an amazing gift, necessarily ... [but] I was upset that Albanese hadn't thought about gift-giving culture because it is very central in Japan.

"For me, the faux pas was really not taking the gift-giving seriously."

However, even for Japanese people, social etiquette around giving and receiving gifts is not straightforward. Eri Dennis, former officer at the Australian embassy in Tokyo and current cultural consultant at manufacturing consultancy Shinka Management, told SBS News the practice is deeply ingrained and "definitely an important part of our culture".

"Whenever we visit someone, even a family member or your friend, for some significant occasion, or if you haven't met them for some time, it's just a natural part of our culture that we bring along gifts," she said. "It doesn't have to be an expensive gift, but it's a gesture that we care about you."

Shizuoka Crown Melons are considered by some in Japan as closer to an art form than a fruit. Much like champagne, the "king of fruit" can only be produced in the Shizuoka prefecture on the south coast, grown in raised beds, hand-pollinated, and massaged to improve their look and sweetness.

Dennis notes that melons — grown throughout Japan with varieties tied to each prefecture — are associated with wealth and considered a "very expensive fruit". Typically, a valuable melon would be presented as a gift with ornate wrapping and placed in a special box.

"Japanese people, we enjoy the beauty of fleeting nature," he said, noting that gifts from nature are also tied up in aspects of Shinto Buddhist cultural understanding.

Shizuoka Crowns have a clean, highly concentrated honey-like flavour and a melt-in-your-mouth texture. Eating them is generally a communal act, shared between the family of those who have been presented with the melon, once it has been chilled in the fridge and the guest has long departed.

Sanae Takaichi brought the melons from Shizuoka for Anthony Albanese in May to mark the relaxation of Australian import standards, allowing their sale in Australia. Source: Supplied / X/@takaichi_sanae

Dennis explains that the agricultural industry has significant sway in Japanese politics and that a gift of fruit or vegetables is also seen as a way to honour the farmers who laboured to produce it. With each region boasting particular types of produce cultivation, regional and national pride stems from the growers themselves.

Yosuke Suzuki, a senior official at Shizuoka Prefecture Greenhouse Agricultural Cooperative, which has been producing Shizuoka Crown Melons since 1921, told SBS News that their cultivation techniques have been passed down through generations.

"One of the distinctive features of our melons is a cultivation method known as "ichiboku ikka" — one fruit per plant. We grow just one melon on each plant, so all the nutrients are concentrated into that single fruit. That allows us to produce an exceptionally delicious melon," he said.

Crown melons are a type of muskmelon, which are so called because they have been bred to omit a fragrant odour that fills the room when cut. They are graded for their appearance and prized for their T-shaped stems, with the most symmetrical melons fetching eye-watering sums at auction.

In 2019, a pair of Yubari King melons grown in Hokkaido sold for ¥5 million ($44,400). More typically, top-grade melons retail for upwards of $300.

"It isn’t just about the taste. We also place great importance on their appearance. The netting pattern on the surface is beautifully and evenly distributed. That is the result of the tremendous care producers put into each melon, tending to them every single day," Suzuki added.

Fruits, like these Yubari melons, have become regional symbols and are gifted as a source of local pride or inter-cultural exchange. They can fetch high prices at auction. This pair sold for ¥3 million ($26,600) in 2024. Source: AFP / Yosuke Hayasaka

Takaichi brought the melons from Shizuoka for Albanese in May in celebration of the Australian import standards being relaxed to allow their sale here. Suzuki notes that his company are targeting 3,000 melons for sale on the domestic market.

High-end Japanese restaurants have already received the first batch of Shizuoka Crowns, according to Japanese media; however, SBS News could not locate any of the recipient restaurants and was told by one high-end importer that they were unaware of the rule change.

On Wednesday, the Opposition referred the issue to the Australian Federal Police, which confirmed to SBS News that it has received correspondence about confidential communications via Japanese official channels.

Dennis doesn't believe that Albanese "did anything wrong", although she can see how describing the gift as "strange" could be seen as disrespectful to some.

"Maybe the older generation might think 'how rude', but I think it's just part of cultural exchange and we move on," she said.

That said, she expects the incident has been an incredible boost to the Japanese melon industry and expects that many Australians will be eager to try the fruit that has caused such a fuss.

title: New Zealand PM Chris Luxon survived a leadership fight, but a greater challenge lies ahead
text:
In brief New Zealand prime minister Chris Luxon survived a leadership fight on Wednesday.

It followed a series of recent gaffes and mis-steps as his National party looks to November's general election.

Chris Luxon will box on as New Zealand prime minister after winning a caucus confidence vote, defying doubters in and outside his party after a run of gaffes that imperilled his premiership.

The National leader called a crunch meeting of his partyroom for Wednesday morning to end speculation around his future.

A leadership change looked on after NZ Herald reported growing dissatisfaction with Luxon's performance, three months out from the 7 November election.

Instead, Luxon emerged victorious from the lengthy meeting, claiming to have united the party and pledging to win a second term for his conservative coalition.

"There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus," he said, in a 75-second appearance without taking questions.

"Now we're going back to work, and we're moving on."

Luxon's office later revealed low-profile defence minister Chris Penk challenged for the leadership in the meeting.

The prime minister then sacked him for doing so, leaving Penk to announce his intention to leave politics at the November election.

Wednesday's vote followed a similar caucus showdown in April, when Luxon brought on and won a confidence vote to silence his critics.

The margin of each vote is a tightly held secret, though media outlets have reported the April result was 27-22 in Luxon's favour.

Rather than Penk, Wellington newspaper The Post reported Erica Stanford, the education minister, was the most likely challenger.

The 48-year-old never confirmed this, and was served a brutal backhander by colleague Nicola Grigg, the minister for women, on the way to the meeting.

"She's a good friend of mine, but she's not a prime minister," Grigg said.

Most observers tipped a successful spill.

One political editor described Luxon's leadership as "hanging by a thread" on Tuesday night, and another rated his survival as "incredibly unlikely", making his victory a defiant and triumphant moment for Luxon.

How did Luxon find himself in this position?

Mentored by party messiah John Key, the 56-year-old former Air New Zealand chief executive enjoyed a meteoric rise in politics.

He entered parliament in 2020, became opposition leader in 2021 and won the 2023 election.

However, he has endured a tough run in the top job, failing to deliver on key campaign pledges to improve New Zealand's misfiring economy and tackle government waste.

His corporate communication style is routinely mocked, and his poor personal popularity is widely seen as a key reason behind National's plunging poll fortunes, from 38 per cent at the election, to a poll average of 29 per cent.

A run of recent gaffes brought about the second leadership vote.

Luxon told battling small business owners in Rotorua they were "negative" and should instead be "retooling and radically disrupting your business".

READ MORE 'Shameful': Outrage as New Zealand scraps its standalone environment department

He also defended his use of a defence force plane to fly home after a party fundraiser — a shocking look for a leader who was forced to return a housing entitlement to stay at his own mortgage-free property.

Luxon has also been pushed around by NZ First leader and foreign minister Winston Peters, who in July caused outrage by telling a China-born Greens MP to "go back to your own country" in parliament.

While Luxon said the 81-year-old maverick's comment was racist, he did not sanction or sack him.

Despite the drama, the National-led coalition remains on course to win re-election on 7 November.

While the contest is tight, the right bloc has consistently kept an edge over the left bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, also known as the Māori Party.

The race has been challenged in recent months by the emergence of newcomer party Opportunity, which hit eight per cent support in a TVNZ poll released on Wednesday.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the leadership shenanigans showed National was in disarray.

"New Zealanders have had a gutful of politicians fighting amongst themselves ... at a time when New Zealanders need them to be fighting for them," he said.

title: 'We're not asking for an easy life': The three key issues at the heart of Australia's 'polycrisis'
text:
IN BRIEF Experts say housing insecurity and climate fears are compounding young Australians' uncertainty about their future.

Young people's belief they can create change improved after the 2025 federal election, a recent report found.

For 24-year-old Sophie Blach, the future feels increasingly difficult to plan.

Working full-time hours in retail and hospitality while undertaking her degree, she said she has been forced to return to her Brisbane family home while she tries to save a deposit to eventually buy a property.

But rising everyday costs mean saving is difficult, leaving her feeling as though the traditional path into adulthood is becoming increasingly out of reach.

"I feel like I'm doing everything you're told you're supposed to do. I'm working, I'm studying, I'm saving when I can," she told SBS News.

"But I wouldn't say my goals feel in reach."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Young Australians are struggling to plan for the future

Sophie's experience reflects a broader trend identified in a new five-year analysis of the Australian Youth Barometer.

The Monash Centre for Youth Policy and Education Practice has tracked more than 2,700 Australians aged 18 to 24 since 2021, examining their experiences across work, education, housing, wellbeing, relationships and civic participation.

READ MORE The surprising factor shaping young Australians' family plans

Its latest report describes young Australians as living through a "polycrisis" of overlapping economic, social, environmental and political pressures that compound one another.

Affordable housing was the biggest issue young people flagged as needing urgent action, rising from 60 per cent in 2022 to 82 per cent in 2025.

Also recognised as needing urgent action was employment opportunities, which rose from 48 in 2022 to 64 per cent in 2025. Climate change was identified as an issue needing urgent action by 44 per cent in 2025, falling from 47 per cent in 2022.

Monash University professor Lucas Walsh, the report's lead author, says the significance of the findings is in how those issues connect.

"These are all embedded within the idea of a polycrisis, which involves overlapping independent events in crisis that intersect and amplify each other," he told SBS News.

Walsh said the study started tracking young Australians at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, providing a five-year window into how their lives and priorities have changed as the country moved through and beyond it.

He describes the pandemic as a "flash of light into more persistent problems" which exposed pressures that were already disproportionately affecting young people.

For Sophie, housing uncertainty isn't isolated from the rest of her life.

Housing and financial pressure are compounding

"I don't necessarily expect to own a house tomorrow, but I would like to feel like it's something I could realistically work towards. It can be discouraging to feel like the goalposts for how much I need to have saved, how much I need to be earning or even spending to get a home keeps changing," she said.

Wendy Stone, a professor of housing and social policy at Swinburne University, told SBS News that secure housing provides the foundation that young people need to establish independence, work, study and relationships.

But she said Australia's housing system is increasingly failing to provide that security, which can affect whether young people can sustain employment or education and even their ability to plan ahead.

"The affordability problem compounds other parts of our system's structural challenges for young people," stone said.

"One of the things that we do know is that the earlier you can get into a secure housing situation, the more likely you are to be able to pursue your education, your employment and your relationships in a way that is sustainable."

Stone said governments need to treat secure, affordable housing as an investment in young people, rather than relying on increased housing supply alone.

She points to targeted housing subsidies for young people undertaking study or training, alongside stronger protections and incentives for long-term renting.

The pressures are also being felt in young people's mental health, with the Barometer finding 99 per cent of the young Australians surveyed reported at least one feeling of anxiety or pessimism in 2025.

Meanwhile, the proportion who sought and received mental-health support fell from 31 per cent in 2021 to 23 per cent in 2025.

Professor of psychiatry Ian Hickie said much of the distress being experienced by young people is connected to practical pressures in their everyday lives.

"A lot of distress is being expressed by young people at the moment has to do with these broader sets of issues that are confronting them on a daily basis," he said.

He said solutions need to be practical measures, from reducing transport costs and providing rental assistance to improving access to health and other essential services.

Climate change adding another layer

Sydney University research fellow Scarlett Smout said young people can feel particularly powerless because they have been "failed by generations preceding them" and now feel they have inherited a problem they have little individual power to solve.

She told SBS News that effective solutions need to create connection and agency, including better access to nature, public transport and community spaces, while making clear that responsibility cannot rest on individuals alone.

"Seeing the government address climate change as a matter of inter-generational inequality but also inter-generational fairness … would hopefully provide some assurance to young people that this matter is being taken seriously and not just the can being kicked down the road."

For Sophie, her concerns can feel inseparable.

"I don't think we're asking for an easy life. We just want to believe that if we work hard, we'll have some control over what happens next," she said.

"In my parents' generation it was more simple, so I didn't think I would be making all these sacrifices and doing all the right things and still not have any reprieve or certainty over what my future will look like. It's demotivating."

Walsh urged governments to respond to these overlapping issues by breaking down siloed policy approaches and, crucially, giving young people a meaningful role in shaping the policies that affect them.

Bleak but not hopeless

The Barometer also found that young people's belief that change is possible improved following the 2025 federal election.

But for Sophie, that hope remains conditional.

"I recognise the privilege we have here in Australia and I do believe there are ways to fix the problems people in my generation are concerned about," she said.

"I try to stay optimistic; it would just help if there was a bit more to be hopeful about, or if it felt like my generation's concerns were actually being prioritised or even considered."

title: A new era for Australia's gig workers? The changes coming for delivery drivers
text:
IN BRIEF On-demand food delivery drivers in Australia will be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 per hour in Australia.

The changes will take effect from 17 August and have been praised by the Transport Workers' Union.

The Fair Work Commission has issued a new minimum standards order for gig workers, including on-demand food, beverage and grocery delivery drivers.

The standards, released on Tuesday, stipulate that on-demand delivery workers must be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 or up to $32 per hour, depending on the type of vehicle used. The order also specifies that delivery platforms must insure workers for on-the-job injuries.

The Transport Workers' Union (TWU), which represents Australian gig workers, said these changes have been years in the making. The TWU initially applied for the minimum standards order in 2024, alongside food delivery platforms Uber Eats and DoorDash.

In a joint statement provided to SBS News, TWU national secretary Michael Kaine described the new standards as "world-leading".

"The world is looking on as gig workers in Australia win new rights and protections that will change their lives, after years of campaigning for a better industry," Kaine said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth also believes the order is a "big step" in providing more robust worker protections.

She said it means "food and delivery workers don't have to trade off flexibility for fairer protections".

The new standards are set to start on Monday 17 August.

Who is covered by the order?

The TWU said "hundreds of thousands" of delivery workers in Australia will be impacted by the new orders.

They specifically apply to employee-like workers who are engaged through digital on-demand delivery platforms — such as Uber Eats and DoorDash — and mainly deliver consumables (food, beverages or liquor) or supermarket groceries.

These workers will be entitled to a guaranteed minimum hourly rate for their "engaged time" between accepting an order and completing the delivery. This is also called an "earnings floor".

People operating bicycles or e-bikes will be paid $31.30 an hour. For motorbikes, this increases to $31.80 per hour, and workers driving cars will earn $32 per hour.

According to the interim order, platforms will calculate a worker's total earnings over a period of up to 21 days. If a worker "has been paid less than the earnings floor in an earnings period, the digital labour platform operator will pay a top-up amount to ... make up the difference", it said.

Right to unpaid time away

The standards also aim to provide a clearer dispute resolution process and workers the right to (unpaid) time away. Key provisions include:

Platforms will establish a feedback forum to enable workers to raise questions or concerns about their work.

If an issue is unable to be resolved between the worker and delivery platform, drivers can refer the dispute to the Fair Work Commission.

Delivery drivers can choose to take "time away" from work without pay.

Time away is at the discretion of workers.

Maggie Lloyd, DoorDash's head of public policy for the Asia-Pacific, Central Asia and the Middle East, described these changes as a "defining moment" for Australia's on-demand economy.

"These new standards prove that strong worker protections and the flexibility that delivery workers value can go hand in hand," Lloyd said in a statement.

Insurance changes

Under the standards, delivery drivers will be responsible for taking out and maintaining compulsory third-party insurance for any vehicles used to provide services. They must also inform their insurer that the vehicle will be used for delivery driving.

Delivery platforms must, at their own expense, take out and maintain a personal accident insurance policy to cover employee-like workers.

Previously, not all workers received these protections because they were considered independent contractors.

Under new standards, Australian food delivery drivers will be granted minimum pay and more protections. Credit: The Feed

In 2023, Uber warned the government that reforms to the gig economy would lead to "catastrophic" job losses. That same year, DoorDash also claimed that food delivery prices could more than triple under a worst-case scenario analysis.

Both companies have since walked back these comments and engaged with the TWU on the new standards.

Ed Kitchen, managing director of Uber Eats in Australia and New Zealand, said he is "proud" to have worked on the industry-first framework.

"This is a great moment for gig workers who play such a critical role in Australia's economy and in the lives of millions of Aussies who rely on food delivery every day."

title: Opposition to promise migration cuts as frontbencher refuses to confirm figure
text:
IN BRIEF The Opposition is expected to propose a policy that would restrict the annual migration rate to 180,000 to aid housing supply.

Andrew Bragg will also introduce the party's national building standards that will apply to new housing.

A senior Coalition frontbencher has refused to confirm specifics of his party's plan to cut migration numbers, despite a formal announcement expected to be made later on Wednesday.

Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg will use a major speech at the National Press Club on Wednesday to call for a cut to net overseas migration levels by nearly half to meet the rate of new housing supply being built.

Treasury modelling published in the May budget expects net overseas migration to fall from 301,000 to 225,000 by the end of this decade.

But the Opposition frontbencher will advocate for an average annual net overseas migration rate of 180,000 to make up for a housing shortfall.

"A [net overseas migration] reduction on this scale is manageable and in line with reductions we have managed in recent history," Bragg will say.

The centrepiece of Bragg's speech will be a commitment to replace the National Construction Code with a new 80-page "Basic Australian Standard".

The Coalition's new standards will focus on cost-effective structural, fire safety and health-related building standards.

"Anything else like mandatory ramps, flattened shower flooring or reinforced walls would be optional extras," Bragg will say.

"The house won't be gold-plated but it won't fall apart. It will be safe."

Labor announced it would freeze the National Construction Code following its productivity roundtable in mid-2026.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil brushed off calls from the Coalition to cut the construction standards to 200 pages earlier in 2026.

"I've talked to builders about that, they laugh their heads off. That is absolutely ridiculous," O'Neil told the National Press Club in May.

The government is not far off presenting a final plan to the building minister later this year to streamline the code, Treasurer Jim Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Wednesday.

title: ‘Has my team’s shooting improved?’ How AI is professionalising junior sport
text:
Advertisement

SportAI ‘Has my team’s shooting improved?’ How AI is professionalising junior sport Marc McGowan Updated August 14, 2026 — 12:26pm ,first published 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

During the dog days of Melbourne’s COVID-19 lockdowns, Sam Hung and his teenage friends would head to a local basketball court and shoot hoops to pass the time. Hung was a high school student back then, but already a budding technological guru. Collingwood junior basketballers are using stat-tracking app Superstat to get better. Jason South With so much time on his hands, he decided to build a basic app that produced shot charts from those street-ball games. Little did he know that experience would be helpful several years later, when he joined forces with Kai Bloomfield and Cordelia King to co-found Superstat. They created a stat-tracking app that uses artificial intelligence computer vision to deliver amateur sports teams – starting with basketball – the kind of performance data previously available only to elite athletes.

Advertisement

Related Article AI Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs Computer vision is an AI subfield that equips machines with the ability to process, analyse and interpret visual inputs such as images and videos, then extract meaningful information. Superstat just scored $3.5 million in seed funding from venture capital firm Blackbird and some private investors, and the team is relocating to Austin, Texas, in September to dive deeper into the United States market – a sports mecca that already is strongly featured among their membership – where they plan to expand to American football, baseball, soccer and volleyball. Closer to home, Australian football and netball are on the company’s hit list, too. “Our mission is to provide pro-level stats for everyone,” Bloomfield told this masthead.

Advertisement

NBA-level stats for amateurs The Melbourne entrepreneurs first worked together on a different app, TrainStop, a sports recruiting matchmaker that was once described as football’s answer to Tinder. The app proved popular with grassroots clubs, but a problem soon surfaced: would-be recruits were “catfishing” them, embellishing their output to try to earn a quick buck. Superstat co-founders Sam Hung, Cordelia King and Kai Bloomfield use AI technology to deliver professional-level statistics for amateur athletes. Eddie Jim Bloomfield, an ex-Oakleigh Chargers development coach in the under-18 Talent League who was working at St Kilda as a football analyst at the time, realised there was a missing link – and it owed to a lack of data.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Australian Open AI analysed Jannik Sinner’s skeleton. This is what it found He was manually “cutting” footage for the Saints, an onerous task mirrored at amateur level, where coaches and fellow volunteers were more time poor and unable to gather the same level of information. Hence, some mischievous TrainStop members saw an opportunity to use that data deficit to their advantage. That was when Bloomfield and co. started wondering about the possibility of using AI to track statistics and plug that gap in grassroots sport. Superstat effectively became the app designed to solve that problem. The company’s early days last year were devoted to football before they found out about Hung’s basketball app from the pandemic.

Advertisement

That was enough for them to pivot to basketball – but it wasn’t until they started attending tournaments and speaking to people involved that they realised the opportunity at hand. The trio recalled a photo they took from the annual Adelaide Easter Classic, where there were four mobile phones positioned on tripods around a court recording a single junior basketball match. Bloomfield, King and Hung plan to expand to many more sports beyond basketball. Eddie Jim Coaches previously spent hours going through vision to manually track statistics, which were often inaccurate because of human error. Those same coaches can now upload footage to Superstat, input basic details such as player numbers, names and jersey colours for AI tagging purposes – and the app does the rest. At the end of the process, users receive an NBA-like box score, including points, rebounds, assists, turnovers, and field goal and free throw attempts, as well as individual minutes played and plus/minus totals for each athlete.

Advertisement

An example of from Superstat’s AI coaching tool. Superstat Superstat also generates team and individual shot charts, and individual player highlights (and lowlights) for coaches to analyse, or parents to send to grandparents. An AI assistant coach offers suggestions on what to focus on at training, too, and answers questions on game trends. The real-life coach could ask something like: “What are my team’s strengths?“. Or, “Has my team’s free throw shooting improved?” or “Where do we need to get better?” The AI assistant coach will then provide an answer, within seconds, from the game data that is uploaded. Using AI technology in this way is a significant step for amateur and junior sport.

Advertisement

Similar basketball analytics and video platforms, such as the US-based Hoopalytics, use AI only for offerings like player evaluations and scouting reports, while still paying human analysts to track the actual statistics. “We thought that a big issue might be that no-one films the games – but everyone does,” Bloomfield said. Superstat hopes to help teams discover the next Josh Giddey. Justin McManus “We want [our app] to kind of be like Strava, with what they’ve done for running and cycling. I’ll use Strava, and it’ll tell me what my next run should be. I feel like an Olympian when I go for my 5km run at my six-minute [per kilometre] pace because I get my VO2 max, my cadence and more. “We want that for player development, and to be able to help players and tell them, ‘Here’s what you’re good at, here’s what you can work on, here’s what to do at training this week’.”

Advertisement

Related Article AFL 2026 AFL stars are being targeted by ‘AI slop’. There’s a sinister motive behind it Among Superstat’s almost 6000 active monthly users is Joe Barker, who coaches one of Collingwood’s under-12 representative teams in the Victorian Junior Basketball League. “What I really like is that it highlights the ‘unsung’ parts of the game that don’t always get recognised – things like rebounds, assists, defensive effort and doing the little things that help the team,” Barker said. “It gives every player a chance to see where they’re contributing, while also giving me useful information to shape training and help the kids improve week to week.” Going beyond the box score

Advertisement

King loves that their app could play a role in recruiting decisions shifting from subjective to objective decisions based on detailed game data. It is part of the vision for the Superstat crew. They have already held discussions with US colleges such as Arizona State, who employ an Australian among their scouting staff. An example of the data generated by the Superstat app. Adobe Stock/supplied Like most sporting organisations, Arizona State have a budget that restricts their recruiting pool to areas they can send scouts to – but Superstat’s AI modelling could change the game in that sense. “The recruitment system in the US is still quite archaic,” King said.

Advertisement

“A lot of it is literally sending YouTube highlights to colleges, and you’ve got to be amazing in the first 30 seconds [to attract attention]. You send a cold email, or DM [direct message], and hopefully, someone sees it. Anything we can do to improve that visibility is a bonus.” Two of Australia’s preeminent experts in AI and sport, Dr Machar Reid and Dr Sam Robertson, don’t believe recruiters have anything to worry about in the foreseeable future. Robertson, who consults for elite sporting organisations and clubs in the US, Europe and Australia on innovation, said AI tagging, which Superstat uses, and its efficiency benefits were this technology’s best use so far. Could AI help sports recruiters better identify the best young talents, such as Richmond’s Sam Lalor? Getty Images However, Robertson was not convinced, at least yet, that AI could positively impact the talent identification process.

Advertisement

Reid, Tennis Australia’s director of innovation, was more optimistic, but agreed with Robertson that using AI to help unearth future stars was “infinitely more complex than just tagging a game”. “The application of AI to talent ID is likely easier and more effective in sports like swimming, tennis, and maybe even golf. So the individual pursuits,” Reid said. “You have a single competitor, perhaps a single technical action to analyse ... there are fewer variables that exist outside your control. From a modelling point of view, the exercise is simpler. “That doesn’t mean it will solve all your dilemmas … but team sports will take a while longer, if indeed they ever get there. You’re always going to, I think, have the human there and that element of heuristics that are important.” That reality has not stopped Superstat’s founders from thinking big.

Advertisement

They hope to take advantage of AI’s rapidly increasing sophistication to one day be able to analyse and measure an athlete’s performance more closely to offer even greater insights. Related Article AI Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg writes 6500-word essay on the future “What we’re looking to build isn’t just a system that’s good on a box score level, but more of a visual level,” chief technology officer Hung said. “We want to be able to identify, ‘If this person’s this tall, and he’s playing in this age group, he should be doing better, or moving this way to perform even better, or help the team in this way’. That’s another layer of data that we’re trying to get to.” Come back next weekend for the second part of this masthead’s series on how AI is changing sport. title: Investor home loans nose dive as they retreat from market
text:

The number of home loans taken out by investors has slumped by almost 9 per cent, new data has revealed. But the figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics reveal the drop is concentrated among investors looking to buy an existing home, with loans for the construction of new properties actually increasing. Investor loans for new construction actually rose, but the number of overall investor loans was down almost 9 per cent. Joe Armao The bureau reported that all loans fell by 5.4 per cent in the June quarter to be just 0.1 per cent up over the past 12 months. Among investors, the fall was 8.6 per cent. Since the start of the year, investor home loans have fallen by 12.9 per cent.

Advertisement

The largest drop has been among loans taken out by investors for an existing property. These fell by 14.8 per cent in the quarter during which the federal government announced its changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The negative gearing change excludes investors who borrow to build a new property. That seems to be having an impact. Loans to investors for a new home grew by 4.4 per cent and hit an all-time high for data that only goes back to 2019. Loading The bureau’s head of finance statistics, Mish Tan, noted that loans taken out by all borrower types had fallen over the past three months.

Advertisement

“Lending conditions continued to change in the June quarter, with the Reserve Bank increasing the cash rate for the third time in 2026. Changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were also announced in the federal budget in May, to commence in July 2027,” she said. Tan noted there was a substantial fall in loans taken out by investors. “The fall in investor loans in the June quarter was the largest fall since September quarter 2022,” she said. “Annually, growth in investor loans slowed from 19.4 per cent in the March quarter to 2.8 per cent this quarter.” The largest drop in investor loans was in NSW, down by 15.5 per cent, while they tumbled by 14.2 per cent in Victoria and by 10.1 per cent in Queensland.

But it is not a national story. Investor loans increased by 12.8 per cent in the Northern Territory, by 8.7 per cent in the ACT and by 5.3 per cent in Tasmania. Related Article Opinion

title: How a 1990s radio quiz helped the Wallabies celebrate their 1000th player
text:
