SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby How a 1990s radio quiz helped the Wallabies celebrate their 1000th player Iain Payten August 14, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sometime on Saturday evening in Townsville, Massimo De Lutiis will be presented with a Test cap in the Wallabies’ dressing room. Like cricket’s Baggy Green, the old-style cap will be green, with gold trim, and the number “1000” will be embroidered on the side. That will be De Lutiis’ Wallaby number (pending his almost-certain entry into the game from the bench), and the presentation will be made by Rugby Australia president – and Wallaby No. 774 – Nathan Sharpe. RA boss Phil Waugh, Wallaby No. 766, will also be in the room. Soon-to-be Wallabies player No. 1000, Massimo de Lutiis, and other Wallaby “centurions” who preceeded him. Graphic: Stephen Kiprillis/Images: Rugby Australia It will be a special moment for De Lutiis, a Gold Coast-raised prop with Italian and Irish heritage. But the debut of the 1000th man to play in a Test for Australia in rugby union will also provide a moment for reflection for all other Wallabies, past and present. “It gives you a perspective of how special it is to be one of the 1000,” Wallabies prop Angus Bell said this week.

Advertisement

Paddy Carew (pictured in 1899) is officially recognised as Wallaby No. 1. Rugby Australia archive What is less appreciated, though, is how we even know De Lutiis will be Wallaby No. 1000, and that Paddy Carew was No. 1, and where Sharpe, Waugh and 996 other players also sit on that list. It turns out this knowledge owes to a Sydney stockbroker who was stumped on a radio quiz show in the early 1990s. Matthew Alvarez has been Rugby Australia’s honorary statistician for a long time, but 33 years ago, he was a sports nut competing in a team on Tracey Holmes’ sports trivia quiz on ABC Grandstand radio. “We got asked a question about who was Australia’s most capped front-row forward,” Alvarez recalls. “At the time, I didn’t know, and I didn’t know where to find the answer. And it was not easy to find. But that triggered the journey.”

Advertisement

For the record, the answer (then) was Andy McIntyre; now it is James Slipper. But the murkiness of the Wallabies’ historical record launched Alvarez on a mission. He set out to produce a definitive list of all Wallabies players, in exact order, from the first Test in 1899, containing debut dates, game stats and as much biographical detail as possible. It would take him a decade to complete. “The difficult thing was being sure enough of the history for the first 100 years to not get to a point where I’d miss somebody, and therefore every other number was wrong,” Alvarez said. Matthew Alvarez, the honorary statistician of Rugby Australia, pictured in Sydney. Steven Siewart

Advertisement

Alvarez trawled through published books and yearbooks on the topic, but finding errors, he painstakingly cross-referenced every Test with available information in libraries, newspaper archives, videos and other historical records. “It was going back through to ensure we had all replacements, and anyone who was capped, and then to go through in an orderly manner and number them from the start, as per what had been done with Australian cricket, whereby they started alphabetically,” Alvarez said. “Their game had been going before ours, so that was a simple benchmark to then number ours accordingly, rather than trying to give it to whoever was wearing jersey No. 1. That was too complicated, because jersey numbering has changed significantly over the years.” Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Wallaby No. 988, after his first cap at Twickenham in 2024. Julius Dimitaga/Rugby Australia So Carew was designated Wallaby No. 1, out of all the players in the first side in 1899 which beat the British Isles 13-3 at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Advertisement

“It took almost 10 good years from the time I started to get to the point where I was comfortable putting the numbers to everyone,” Alvarez said. The complete Wallaby list was first published in Inside Rugby magazine in 2002 (with Dan Vickerman the most recent Wallaby at the time, No. 777). It was later embraced by the Australian Rugby Union as the official list. All the Wallaby player numbers for new players – and retrospectively to those who’d come before – are based on Alvarez’s master document. Vic Richards, Wallaby No. 300, playing for Randwick in 1935. Sydney Morning Herald Archive The rules were (and are) simple: you become a capped Wallaby when you run on the field in a Test, and your number is based on alphabetical order if you run on at the same time as another debutant, be it in a starting XV or in a group of substitutes. Figuring out the order of substitutes was sometimes tricky, particularly for those games with limited records and/or video. Wallaby numbers are now entrenched in the game, and are referenced heavily by the Wallabies and the Classic Wallabies. They are cherished by players, a number of whom have tattoos, safely due to Alvarez’s diligence.

Advertisement

But most have no idea that the Wallaby number concept is relatively new. That includes former Test centre Adam Ashley-Cooper, who is a former milestone man as Wallaby No. 800. The “centurions” provide a nice snapshot of Wallabies history, and four are living: Chris “Buddha” Handy was 600 in 1978, Peter Jorgensen (700 in 1992), Ashley-Cooper and Sefa Naivalu (900 in 2017). Ashley-Cooper’s manic debut in 2005 is almost folklore. The young centre from the NSW Central Coast was travelling with the Wallabies as a development player when he was named as an emergency reserve for a Test against South Africa in Perth.

Advertisement

When Elton Flatley lost vision in the warm-up, Ashley-Cooper (AAC) was rushed out of the stands to get a jersey and boots and join the bench. The after-dinner story goes that AAC had downed a pie and a beer already, and he adds another pie and beer with each telling. Adam Ashley-Cooper on debut in 2005. Getty Images Wearing a jersey without a number, he became Wallaby No. 800 with a few minutes on the field at the end of the Test, when Clyde Rathbone went down with a “cork”. “That was the code among players back in the day,” Ashley-Cooper said. “You did what you could to get a debutant on. I did the same for two blokes later on in my career: Ben Tapuai and Pat McCabe.” Ashley-Cooper had to borrow the suit of assistant coach Scott Wisemantel to receive his Test cap post-match.

Advertisement

“I was thinking, ‘What the f--- just happened?’ – it was such a whirlwind,” he said. Ashley-Cooper’s debut even became a trivia question on a Tooheys bottle cap, which his father Tony proudly showed him a few years later. Who is the only Wallaby to debut without a number on his back? “He goes, ‘You’ve made it’, and I’m like, “Mate, I’ve played over 50 games for the Wallabies’, and he says, ‘This is my proudest moment!’,” Ashley-Cooper says with a laugh. Ashley-Cooper played 121 Tests for the Wallabies, a rarity for all the centurion milestone men. Most only played a handful.

Advertisement

But that, too, is consistent with Alvarez’s data. The average Test tally for a Wallaby over 127 years is 13 Tests, and even that’s been inflated by an explosion of Tests in the professional era. Before 1996, the average was eight Tests. Related Article Updated

Australian rugby Kiss flags big change to Wallabies’ attack after major reshuffle for Japan rematch “More than 18 per cent of all Wallabies (185) have only played one test,” Alvarez notes. “And more than 40 per cent have played three or fewer tests.” The average career lasts for 2½ years, and the 1920s, when rugby was rebuilding after a war that took the lives of 500 Australian rugby players, was the decade with the most debutants, at 121. In 126 years and 717 Test matches, the average age of all Wallabies debutants has been 23.8.

Advertisement

De Lutiis is ahead of the curve, at 22, and his career length is yet to be determined. But one thing seems certain: you can bank on Massimo De Lutiis, Wallaby No. 1000, being the answer to a trivia question. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: Pigeons will love Clover’s $150m vision for Town Hall. We might prefer a food court
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWSydney Opinion Pigeons will love Clover’s $150m vision for Town Hall. We might prefer a food court Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist August 14, 2026 — 11:30am

August 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Like Clover Moore, we all love a square, or at least the idea of one. The City of Sydney has just unleashed its plans for a big beautiful square in front of Sydney Town Hall, the fruit of a 40-year plan to replace the existing buildings around the intersection of George, Park and Druitt streets with our own Piazza San Marco. The $150 million budget has been criticised, but the council says it has long factored this into its plan and points to the re-pedestrianising of George Street as a model of economic cost-benefit. The design for the 4500-square metre square, with 30 trees, “an interactive water feature” and fixed and movable chairs, expresses the council’s vision: “Like other great global cities, Sydney needs well-designed public spaces where people can come together, spend time and connect. A civic heart belongs to everyone – a welcoming place where everyday moments and civic life sit side by side.” An artist’s impression of the proposed square opposite Sydney Town Hall. Choi Render The Lord Mayor, Clover Moore, who has dedicated much of her 21-year tenure to increasing shared public spaces, says, “All the people now living in the city will enjoy it very much. It’ll be a Trafalgar Square, a Piccadilly Square, like Piazza San Marco in Venice.” The new square will open up views of some of the city’s historic buildings such as Sydney Town Hall, St Andrews

Cathedral and the Queen Victoria Building (and, um, the Citigroup and Ausgrid towers). Ah, the idea of a square. Old nonnas gossiping over a coffee in the morning, kids chasing balls during the day, open-air aperitifs in the twilight. In Europe, which the lord mayor likes to reference, the culture of town squares is a direct rebuttal to the Donald Trump-JD Vance lecture series on a continent “going to hell”. (If they want to see a culture going to hell, have they tried visiting the USA?)

Advertisement

But then, you might also wonder when our own visionaries last visited Europe and Britain. Trafalgar Square is a nasty roundabout jammed with open-top tourist buses and menaced by a ring of Pret A Mangers and Caffe Neros. It compares unfavourably with Trafalgar Square in Marsfield, which at least has ample parking and a bottle shop. “Piccadilly Square” is not a thing, but Piccadilly Circus is another commuter hellscape where people have to wear their mobile phones on wires around their necks while photographing the Eros statue to stop them being stolen. And Piazza San Marco might have been the “drawing room of Europe” when Napoleon was there 220 years ago, but today if you want to escape getting caught up in a group trailing after a flag, your only option is to flee into a queue for a $12 espresso. Related Article Exclusive

City life First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square Only in our dreams is the big European city square what we want it to be. In Paris and Rome, the Notre Dame and Louvre forecourts and St Peter’s Square are congested, configured around metal barricades, places you go to obey police and stand in lines. Istanbul’s Taksim Square is an intersection, and in Florence’s Piazza della Signoria you can watch the world go by in the guise of monstrous facial surgeries, American nepo babies and Ferragamo bags. The ideal European squares are not the famous ones; they’re the small ones in big towns or the big ones in small towns. In square-filled cities like Madrid, Bologna and Brussels, the main square is the crappiest one, the retail and restaurant culture blighted by extortionate rents and overtourism. The squares that still manage to embody our ideals are the little out-of-the-way ones, with old cafes and bars and communities centred usually around churches, where competition does not dictate behaviour and where you can be as contented-looking as the folk in the City of Sydney’s artists’ impressions of its new square. It’s a dream, but it’s not in the middle of the big city and it’s contained in complex cultural traditions rather than utopian social engineering. Which brings me to my point, which is that a town square is cultural more than physical. Small squares based around the way people live in apartment cities, “where people come together, spend time and connect”, have emerged organically over time. A big square can’t magically invent those customs: at best, it can only express what is already in the culture. The new square, says the lord mayor, isn’t going to try to copy the European ones; it’s “going to be very Sydney and it’s going to be very Australian”.

Advertisement

But what does that mean? How do Sydney’s built public spaces express who we are? Pedestrian malls like the Manly Corso, Oxford Street Mall in Bondi Junction and Parramatta Square hardly bring to life the vision splendid. Stepping out of the way of oncoming ebikes and wiping the bird poo off the public seats, our mall life is hobbled by the Australian disease of high rents and short-term retail tenancies. In 20 years, our summertime climate will have turned concrete outdoor squares into no-go zones. Trafalgar Square’s water fountains were fenced off this week amid 36C temperatures during the fifth heatwave to hit England this European summer. Getty Images If the City of Sydney wanted to study how we actually use public spaces, it might look out the window. A pebblecrete wasteland, home to the homeless, Town Hall Square could be Sussan Ley’s next project when she wants to see how the Australian other half lives. Town Hall Square belongs to that 20th-century utopian planning notion that if you build an open space you will change people’s behaviour; architecture can create community. In Town Hall Square, architecture has created a community for pigeons and a small quota of allowable protesters, largely a place people rush through as if avoiding sniper fire. Finally admitting defeat on Town Hall Square, the council is to refurbish it next year as “Sydney Square”, a new experiment to see if removing pebblecrete and changing a name can re-engineer the way we live. As much as we would like to see the $150 million square, which will have a “Sydney Aboriginal” name, realise the council’s 40-year vision, it’s also possible that Sydney people just don’t do public squares. We do Westfields and food courts, we do parks and green spaces (sometimes), we do sports grounds and fish markets, but throughout the Sydney suburbs our built public spaces are often dispiritingly windswept and avoidable, a disappointment to the dreams of those who planned them.

Advertisement

The City of Sydney envisions “a lively gathering place for generations to come”. In its artists’ impressions of the new square, those generations walk, talk and smile, or (Clover Moore’s words) sit as they already do on George Street “on those seats every day under the trees, looking at the flowers, chatting to their friends”. In the drawings, not a single one is doing what Sydney people actually do, which is rush somewhere else, scarf takeaway while wearing earpods, or sit in a Talmudic hunch over their phones, living their lives in the virtual town square, the only one they know. Do we want public squares – or food courts? Cole Bennetts Nobody in the artists’ picture is squabbling over a table, nobody is dealing with a previous occupant’s rubbish, and nobody is staring blank-eyed at the overpriced coffee and muffin they have just been forced to acquire from the chain eateries which are the only ones that can afford the surrounding rents. It’s hardly the Europhile vision, but here we go, we’re optimists, always ready to give ourselves another try. Malcolm Knox is a journalist, author and columnist. title: Disney diehards take their fandom to infinity, and beyond
text:
Advertisement

CultureMoviesDisney Disney diehards take their fandom to infinity, and beyond Michael Idato August 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

By the time you’re reading this, tens of thousands of Disney fans will be pushing through the turnstiles at the studio’s D23 convention in Anaheim, California, the House of Mouse spin-off to San Diego Comic-Con which draws Disney diehards from around the world. They have come to meet the stars of Disney projects, see and hear first-look trailers and announcements, and buy toys. Lots and lots of toys. D23, a one-stop shop which merges branded marketing and old-school fan convention, is as renowned for its cosplaying fans as it is for the nearby Honda Stadium showcases, which will, over this weekend, unveil the next two years of Disney’s plans in the realms of streaming TV, animated and live-action movies, and theme park and cruise attractions. Think of them as Hillsong for plush toys and roller coasters. Happy clappers? Disney fans worshipping at the altar of the House of Mouse in 2024. So, what is likely to lead the headlines? The most anticipated drop is likely to be either a teaser trailer or a glimpse of production footage from Star Wars: Starfighter. The film, produced by Disney-owned Lucasfilm and set five years after the events of Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker, will star Ryan Gosling and is expected in cinemas in 2027. That makes this year’s D23 the most likely staging ground to start marketing it to Disney-brand diehards. A year out from release and so far, not a single frame marketed to the audience? That’s an oversight. Expect it to be corrected. Directed by Shawn Levy and written by Jonathan Tropper, the film also has an intriguing supporting cast: Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Aaron Pierre and Amy Adams among them.

Advertisement

Marvel’s big ticket announcement is likely to be X-Men related, specifically the upcoming reboot directed by Jake Schreier. What makes that significant? Schreier’s last film Thunderbolts was a refreshing spin on the Marvel universe, which is beginning to show its age in story and casting terms. Gift with purchase: it’s written by Lee Sung Jin (Beef) and Joanna Calo (The Bear). Two buzzier writers you will not find. On the X-Men front, there is already persistent online chatter. Sadie Sink is tipped to play telepathic and telekinetic Jean Grey, Kit Connors has been tipped to play Cyclops and Samara Weaving is tipped to play diamond-hard super heroine Emma Frost. Marvel’s Kevin Feige is expected to confirm those castings, and unveil more. But there’s less urgency here; the X-Men reboot is not due in cinemas until late 2028. Feeling the call of the Force: Star Wars fans at a “cosplay meetup” at D23. The Disney animation headliner will almost certainly be Hexed, the studio’s upcoming supernatural coming-of-age film about a young witch discovering her powers. Disney unveiled the voice cast and a glimpse of the film at the CinemaCon convention in Las Vegas. Audiences at D23 are expected to be given an extensive preview of the film. But rumours suggest Disney is also likely to tap its legacy well, with news about a third instalment of the Frozen franchise. Late 2027 is the date earmarked for the film, and this year’s D23 is a critical step; D23 only happens every other year, and next year’s marketing calendar will be dominated by the 50th anniversary of Star Wars.

Advertisement

Disney is expected to showcase a couple of other Lucasfilm and Marvel titles. The second season of the Star Wars series Ahsoka is long overdue, and a new trailer is likely to drop. The second season is due early in 2027, and in a highly competitive space like D23 (and it’s non-Disney cousin, San Diego Comic-Con) buzz doesn’t come cheap. Marvel is also expected to drop footage from this year’s Avengers: Doomsday. With a December release date, that film might as well be opening next week for the time left to ramp the marketing noise up a notch. And critically, coming off big box office returns for The Odyssey, Moana and Spider-Man, “nobody goes to the movies” is wearing thin as an excuse for underperforming films. Rosario Dawson as Ahsoka Tano. The show’s second season is expected to be among this year’s big reveals. Lucasfilm Though the convention is pitched wider than the company’s streaming assets, all roads lead ultimately to an arms race in the digital television space. Disney’s core asset is threefold: Disney+, the US-based Hulu and ESPN+ which command, between them, a paid subscriber base of around 207 million people worldwide. The market leader, and logically Disney’s major competitor, Netflix, has more than 325 million subscribers worldwide. That looks like a commanding margin, however, Netflix’s core assets lack the pop culture appeal of Disney’s. Marvel and Star Wars are, after all, hard to argue with.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks While major announcements will make headlines in the mainstream media, D23 also feeds a raft of very detailed reveals to a micro-economy of Disney-focused news websites and blogs, YouTube channels and fan podcasts, with names like All Ears, Blog Mickey and Mice Chat, which unpack content announcements and theme park developments in minute detail. The dozen or so most-read of those sites generate as many as 100 million page views on a busy month, with more than 120 million subscribers to major social video channels across YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. If measured as a single consolidated vertical, that micro-economy is worth more than US$300 million. Of particular interest to those sites will be the company’s plans for new theme park extensions, including Villain’s Land, the most substantial addition to a Disney parks since the launch the Star Wars-themed Galaxy’s Edge in 2019. Villain’s Land, at Walt Disney World in Florida, will be themed entirely around the villains of Disney stories, including Maleficent (Sleeping Beauty), Ursula (The Little Mermaid) and Jafar (Aladdin). D23 is held every other year in Anaheim, California. The event draws as many as 100,000 people through its gates across a three-day weekend, excluding a separate D23 Disneyland day and, this year, a D23-branded baseball match at Dodger Stadium. The injection of revenue into the local economy, including accommodation, dining, transport and retail is worth an estimated US$55 million.

title: For Geelong, the safest path on Kolodjashnij was the hardest. They took the easy way
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion For Geelong, the safest path on Kolodjashnij was the hardest. They took the easy way Darren Kane Sports Columnist August 14, 2026 — 11:30am

August 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Everyone walking upright has this week opined on the vexed matter of Jake Kolodjashnij and his treatment by his employer, the Geelong Football Club. To recap, Kolodjashnij, a 30-year-old player with a history of concussive incidents, signed a waiver that saw him assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries in a secret deal with the Cats that was not approved by the AFL. Loading The latest development, of the AFL Commission instructing an independent lawyer to determine whether the clubhas contravened any AFL rule, is important. It’s equally irrespective. Kolodjashnij’s injury history was in 2024 examined by the AFL’s concussion panel, which effectively green-lighted him to continue playing. That isn’t the same as being given an entirely clean bill of health. These things can be inconclusive and not sufficient to end a player’s career, but at the same time problematic.

Advertisement

What seems to have occurred next, though, is perplexing. In circumstances where AFL players are excluded from statutory worker’s compensation schemes, and where it’s vanishingly impossible for them to secure alternate coverage in the insurance marketplace that includes cover for head trauma and latent-onset neurological conditions, the Cats asked the player to execute a document as a condition of continued employment. A document which apparently included provisions regarding Kolodjashnij’s informed consent (ie, an acknowledgement of what he would be exposing himself to by continuing to play) and what has been portrayed as a “liability waiver”, purported to exonerate the club. Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij. Getty This document – also, apparently – was produced under a cloak of secrecy, to the point it wasn’t disclosed to the AFL Players Association nor registered with the AFL. To me, that’s troubling stuff.If Geelong felt it had nothing to fear, why did its guiding minds think it had anything to hide? If it’s true that there’s a chain of email correspondence between the AFL and the club about the concept and development of this document, then that’s relevant evidence but doesn’t free anyone from blame. Sporting rules are one thing, but one thing only.

Advertisement

The better focus is on asking what was going on inside the minds of those who signed off on this arrangement. The Geelong Football Club is a company. The Corporations Act requires that directors and officers of companies exercise their powers and discharge their duties with the degree of care and diligence a reasonable person would if they were a director or officer of a company in the same circumstances. Legislation is, of course, for the courts to interpret. The test is not whether the directors did the right thing: Instead, it’s a question of was the decision, viewed prospectively, one that a reasonably careful director could make having regard to the risks and potential benefits? On one side of the ledger is the prospect of continued services being provided by an experienced and, evidently, excellent footballer. On the other side sit the risks of brain injuries being sustained by an uninsurable player, and the associated risks and harm that might flow. If what Kolodjashnij signed does incorporate words amounting to a “waiver”, in my experience clients don’t routinely instruct lawyers to draft special contractual waivers for risks never foreseen. The concealment of the waiver from the AFL and AFLPA – whether by deceitful intention, or a systems failure– strains the notion of any of this being implemented in good faith and for a proper purpose. Again, if you’ve nothing to fear you’ve nothing to hide. Further, the Corporations Act also requires directors and officers more generally to exercise their powers and discharge their duties in good faith, for a proper purpose and in the best interests of the company. In the context of a professional sporting franchise, these “best interests” extend beyond filling shelves of a trophy cabinet. Consider its covenant with its 90,000-odd members, and its duty of candour.

Advertisement

Ask yourself again – is it in good faith and proper, for Geelong’s directors and senior management to have proceeded down this path? Knowing the apparent risks to which the player would be exposed? Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 Kolodjashnij told me about his ‘tough conversations’. His case reveals much bigger issues Moreover, did those guiding minds turn to the question of whether this clandestine arrangement had any legal force? AFL standard playing contracts, buttressed by the collective bargaining agreement, do not permit “side deals” as to the reapportionment of legal liability. The contracting arrangements certainly don’t countenance the idea of secret deals. It’s hardly certain this document would be enforceable. Moreover, a release signed in 2024 doesn’t easily swallow a neurodegenerative disease manifesting in 2046, absent the clearest imaginable words. Aside from any other factor, how could one satisfactorily demonstrate that what Kolodjashnij was exposed to before executing the document did not matter? Further, it’s express under the CBA that AFL clubs provide and maintain safe working environments for players as far as is reasonably practicable. That’s consistent with the Victorian statutory position under the Occupational Health and Safety Act.

Advertisement

The words “reasonably practicable” constitute a defined calculus. This refers to the likelihood of the hazard, the degree of harm, what the employer knows or ought to know, and the availability and cost of controls. What’s absent is the matter of the employee’s consent. These workplace duties are criminal in character, owed by the employer to the state and prosecuted by the regulator. The duties aren’t in the nature of private rights a footballer can bargain away, which is why a signed release isn’t an answer to any prosecution. The OH&S Act asks whether the risk was eliminated or reduced, where a “waiver” achieves neither, and instead is a liability instrument masquerading as something else. Overall, though, the best question here that directors should ask, is not merely can we do this, but should we? For the law of directors’ duties sets a floor, not a licence. And here’s where the analysis ceases being merely legal, because duties were never designed as a ceiling on conscience. The genuinely hard decisions in any boardroom aren’t choices between right and wrong; they’re choices between defensible and right. It strikes me that Geelong’s board had three roads to choose to roll down. The easy road, which it seemingly did. The middle road, of disclosing this special arrangement to the AFL and the AFLPA, and letting the sun shine on it. Or the hard road, of sitting with Jake Kolodjashnij, his manager and his family, and having the difficult, career-ending and tear-stained conversation.

Advertisement

The perverse elegance here, is that the hardest road was simultaneously the safest one to traverse; legally, ethically and reputationally. The concept of courage appears nowhere in the Corporations Act, yet it’s the substrate on which every duty in the legislation depends – because a director who can’t say the hardest word has outsourced the job to whoever can. None of this is a charge against Kolodjashnij; nor entirely against the individuals on Geelong’s board, several of whom are experienced, decent directors – who I suspect know precisely how this looks. Rather, it’s a charge against a system that abandons clubs and players in a room with an uninsurable risk; and against a boardroom culture that mistook a defensible YES for quite possibly a contrary, correct answer.

title: The next person chosen to help decide mortgage rates
text:
The head of a public policy think tank who used to be the business lobby's chief economist has been unveiled as the newest member of the influential nine-member board responsible for setting interest rates in Australia.

Melinda Cilento, chief executive of the Committee for Economic Development of Australia, was appointed to the Reserve Bank's monetary policy board by Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Friday.

A former chief economist at the Business Council of Australia, Ms Cilento will start her five-year term in the role, replacing the outgoing Ian Harper, on September 1.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She has also served as a board member at oil and gas giant Woodside, Wesfarmers Insurance and health insurer Australian Unity.

Ian Harper will leave his role on the Reserve Bank's monetary policy board in September. (James Ross/AAP PHOTOS)

Dr Chalmers said her appointment followed a thorough and considered selection process, including consultation with the opposition.

"Melinda Cilento is a highly respected economist with broad and deep expertise and experience," he said in a statement.

"This appointment will help ensure the Board has the right mix of skills and perspectives."

Ms Cilento was chosen from a shortlist of candidates compiled by RBA governor Michele Bullock, Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson, and former Prime Minister's Department secretary Martin Parkinson.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Along with ex-officio board member Ms Wilkinson, Ms Cilento joins other Labor appointees Marnie Baker, Renee Fry-McKibbin, Iain Ross, Bruce Preston and deputy governor Andrew Hauser.

Only Ms Bullock, who was appointed to the board by former treasurer Josh Frydenberg before becoming chair, and Carolyn Hewson remain from the previous Liberal government.

Like Ms Bullock, Ms Cilento has lamented Australia's weak productivity growth for causing living standards to stagnate.

She has also spoken about the need to address intergenerational inequity, welcoming Labor's efforts to curb tax breaks for property investors in the federal budget.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Her first test in the new role will come at the RBA board's next meeting on September 29.

Michele Bullock's hawkish commentary this week has left the door open to another rate hike. (Susie Dodds/AAP PHOTOS)

Markets are fully priced in for another hold in September, after the central bank kept the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent on Tuesday.

But Ms Bullock's hawkish commentary following the decision left the door open to another hike, keeping the November meeting live to the possibility of another rate rise.

"We've already raised three times, and we will go again if we need to," she told reporters following the meeting.

"And I think personally that it's quite possible we might need to go, but we'll wait and see what the data tells."

title: 'Over the top': PM urges gambling inducement crackdown
text:
Inducements from gambling companies to keep people having a punt are excessive and should be stopped, the prime minister says.

As the federal government and coalition edge closer to a deal on betting reform, Anthony Albanese said measures needed to be put in place to tackle gambling addiction.

The prime minister said he was confident of the reforms being able to pass parliament in the coming week

"(Inducements) are over the top and they need to be wound back. In particular, some of the inducements that will encourage people into the system are just not on," he told reporters in Canberra on Friday.

Anthony Albanese is confident the government's gambling reforms will pass parliament. (Mick Tsikas/AAP PHOTOS)

"The problem is addiction, and when someone has an addiction, if there are inducements that are encouraging that addiction, that's a bad thing."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The comments followed a Senate inquiry which heard gambling companies plied customers with drugs and sex workers to keep on the platform.

The sites, such as Sportsbet and Tabcorp, have denied the allegations.

Betting firms Sportsbet and Tabcorp were named in a Senate inquiry as firms that offered drugs. (Darren England/AAP PHOTOS)

Labor is attempting pass reforms through parliament which would ban gambling ads between 6am and 8.30pm, as well as stop the ads in stadiums, on player jersey and during live sport broadcasts.

However, it has come under fire for not implementing a full ban, as recommended by late Labor MP Peta Murphy in a landmark report handed down in 2023.

Labor would need the support of either the Greens or coalition to get the changes through the Senate.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Any deal on the reforms is likely to be announced after a Senate inquiry report into the reforms is handed down on Monday.

A vote on the reforms is then set to be held in the lower house on Tuesday, with a deal more likely to be reached with the coalition.

Mr Albanese said talks on the issue had been constructive.

"We will also look in the amendments that we're considering, and we'll go through our process respectfully in our caucus, as will other parties," he said.

"There's nothing wrong with people having a punt on a Saturday, there's nothing wrong with people having a beer after work. The problem is if it's an addiction."
